@state-graph/glossary.entries.brief.body: The first time you enter a level, a few pages of Intro open first, explaining the level’s new problem and anything new in it. To read them again, click “Intro” in the top bar; on a computer, ← and → turn the pages.
In the level’s brief, the Goal says what the level wants worked out, and How to play says what you have to do. When you are stuck, read the goal again first.
Some levels come in several stages, asking a few questions in a row about the same map; some stages hand their circuit board on to the next.
Not every level needs a circuit: in some you draw arrows, fill in numbers or trace routes on the board by hand, and “How to play” says which.
@state-graph/glossary.entries.brief.titl: Intro, goal and how to play
@state-graph/glossary.entries.map.body.0: The levels sit on the map in chapters, and each chapter answers one question. Pass a level and the levels after it open; where the path splits, take the branches in any order, and pass them all to go on.
@state-graph/glossary.entries.map.body.1: The map also has your Parts and this Encyclopedia.
@state-graph/glossary.entries.map.title: Level map
@state-graph/glossary.entries.models.bod: Each level decides which robot model it uses. The first time a new model turns up, the Intro introduces it.

The biggest difference between models is their vision. Boxy sees the ring of cells around it, 3×3; Farsight sees two rings, 5×5. A circuit board can only read cells in view, so reading further takes a different model.
@state-graph/glossary.entries.robot.body: In circuit-board levels the computing is done by a robot. It walks the whole table cell by cell, runs the same circuit board on every cell, and writes the result into the cell it stands on.

The red frame in the middle of the robot’s view is the cell it stands on. For the circuit board to read a cell in view, click it in the view: the “View” part on the left of the circuit board gains an output that reads it, and a cell being read has a blue frame in the view. Cells beyond the table show “out”, and what they send is “—”.
The This cell panel under the view lists facts about the cell. Click one, and the “This cell” part gains an output that reads it.
@state-graph/glossary.entries.robotBoard: Connect an output from View or Cell Info to a computation part, then wire the result to the write-back port. The robot runs the board again at each cell.
After wiring the board, switch tests to check the results across the table. If only a few cells are wrong, start by looking at what the robot reads at those cells.

image/glossary.entries.details.body.1: Hover over a picture to read the value in each cell and the value expected there. When the output is a single number, the expected value, the allowed range and your reading are drawn on one scale; when it is a single row, it is drawn as a curve, with an allowed band round the expected curve.
image/glossary.entries.details.body.2: Whichever test is selected, every part on the board shows its results for that test. On a phone, tap the test tabs along the top to switch, and find the details under “Test details” in the bottom bar.
image/glossary.entries.details.title: Test details
image/glossary.entries.score.body.0: An image circuit can be scored by its part count and computation per output pixel.
image/glossary.entries.score.body.1: After passing the tests, you can reduce computation or part count.
image/glossary.entries.score.body.2: When a task specifies a limit, the circuit must satisfy it as well as pass the tests.
image/glossary.entries.score.title: Scoring and limits
image/glossary.entries.tests.body.0: Each level has a few tests, and each test is an input with its expected output. Your output is compared with the expected one cell by cell: each cell may be off by a tiny amount (the tolerance), and the size must match too. Some levels let a few cells be wrong.
image/glossary.entries.tests.body.1: The results on the parts update all the time, but whether they pass only counts once you press “Run tests”. When every test passes, the level is complete; if not, the first failing test is selected for you. After any change to the circuit, the tests need running again.
image/glossary.entries.tests.body.2: Many levels also have hidden tests: they are checked on every run, but you only learn how many failed, and they are shown once you pass. If every visible test passes but a hidden one fails, your circuit may only happen to work on those particular pictures.
image/glossary.entries.tests.title: Tests and hidden tests
image/glossary.entries.training.body.0: With learnable parts, some weights in a circuit are no longer filled in by you but tuned by the machine. Whenever a circuit contains such a part, two buttons appear: “Train 1 step” and “Train 10 steps”.
image/glossary.entries.training.body.1: Each training step nudges every learnable weight a little in the direction that makes the error smaller. The loss curve beside the buttons shows how the error changes, on a log scale.
image/glossary.entries.training.body.2: Training only sees the visible tests, so the hidden tests check whether what it learned also holds for new pictures. Clearing the circuit starts the weights and the loss curve afresh.
image/glossary.entries.training.body.3: Some levels list a few "new samples": they take no part in training and are only checked, and the panel draws an extra error line for them. Some levels let you choose the learning rate yourself: how big each step is.
image/glossary.entries.training.title: Training
image/glossary.entries.views.body.0: The same data can be viewed as a readout, waveform, grayscale image, relief, cross-section, spectrum, or gradient.
image/glossary.entries.views.body.1: Choose a view to inspect different features of the data, such as changes in brightness or frequency strength.
image/glossary.entries.views.body.2: Change the view for one part or the whole canvas. This leaves the circuit unchanged.
image/glossary.entries.views.title: Views

state-graph/glossary.entries.backtrack.b: The table tells you what the best result is, but not straight out how to get it. Yet every cell’s number came from one of its ways in: the table has also kept every choice.

Start at the end and ask “which way in did this cell’s number come from?”, step back to that cell, and ask again, all the way back to the start: you have recovered the whole route. Working backwards like this is called backtracking.
state-graph/glossary.entries.base.body.0: A rule has to start somewhere. Small problems that need no further breaking down, like the start, have answers that are simply given; these are the base cases. Standing at the start, for instance, counts as 1 route.
state-graph/glossary.entries.base.body.1: Along the edges of the table, some ways in fall outside it; there is no road there, and that shows as “—”. The rule has to cope with these “—”s, or the edge cells come out wrong.
state-graph/glossary.entries.base.body.2: Get a base case wrong and every cell after it goes wrong too. When a test fails, look at the start and the edge cells first.
state-graph/glossary.entries.base.title: Base cases
state-graph/glossary.entries.coin.body.0: Making up an amount from coins of a few values, what is the fewest number of coins? And how many ways are there to pay? Cell i holds the answer for i.
state-graph/glossary.entries.coin.body.1: Look only at the last coin: it could be any of the values, so the ways in are “one coin of each kind taken back”. The same table answers both “the fewest coins” and “how many ways to pay”.
state-graph/glossary.entries.coin.body.2: The table only records how much has been made up, not which coins were used, so the ways it counts treat a different order of paying as a different way.
state-graph/glossary.entries.coin.title: Making change
state-graph/glossary.entries.countOpt.bo: The same skeleton answers different questions. To ask how many, add up all the ways in; to ask what is best, pick the best of the ways in, then count in this cell’s own cost.
On the circuit board, the difference is often just the Merger’s operation: “sum” counts, “min” finds the fewest, “max” finds the most.
Optimising can be broken down like this because every stretch of a best route is itself the best way to reach the end of that stretch. This is called optimal substructure.
state-graph/glossary.entries.counterexam: To prove a state design falls short, you only need one counterexample: two histories that land in the same state but have different futures.
A counterexample does more than show something is wrong; it points to the fix: whatever the two histories differ in is what the state should also remember.
state-graph/glossary.entries.dag.body.0: Think of each cell as a small question and each arrow as “this question needs that answer”, and you have a dependency graph. The cell an arrow starts from must always be worked out before the cell it ends at.
state-graph/glossary.entries.dag.body.1: The graph must have no loops: if A waits for B while B waits for A, neither can ever be worked out. A graph whose arrows have a direction and never loop round is called a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
state-graph/glossary.entries.dag.body.2: Behind a table there is a graph like this too: each cell is a state, and arrows point into it from the cells it reads. That is the “state graph” in the game’s name.
state-graph/glossary.entries.dag.title: Dependency graph
state-graph/glossary.entries.dp.body.0: Dynamic programming is a way of solving problems: break a big problem into small ones, solve the small ones first and write their answers in a table, then build the big answer out of them.
state-graph/glossary.entries.dp.body.1: The small problems are called subproblems. “How many routes lead to school?” breaks down into “how many routes lead to each stop just before school?”, and those break down again, all the way back to the start.
state-graph/glossary.entries.dp.body.2: The name sounds grand, but the doing is just filling in a table: each cell is worked out once, written down, and simply looked up by the cells that come after it.
state-graph/glossary.entries.dp.title: Dynamic programming
state-graph/glossary.entries.edit.body.0: Changing one word into another, deleting, inserting or replacing one letter per step, what is the fewest number of steps? That number is the edit distance.
state-graph/glossary.entries.edit.body.1: It uses the alignment table too. Each of a cell’s ways in stands for one kind of change, and each carries its own cost; pick the cheapest. The same table with a different circuit board answers a different question.
state-graph/glossary.entries.edit.body.2: Spelling correction and the search box’s “did you mean…?” both work out the edit distance from what you typed to each candidate word and pick the closest.
state-graph/glossary.entries.edit.title: Edit distance
state-graph/glossary.entries.expectation: When the outcome is uncertain, an action’s value is the sum of its possible outcomes, each weighted by how likely it is; this is the . With an 80% chance of going right and 20% of going down, say, it is 0.8 × right + 0.2 × down.

Problems where every decision is made under uncertainty are called Markov decision processes, the mathematical skeleton of reinforcement learning. The rule is the familiar one: work out each action’s expectation, pick the best, discount it, and scan until it settles.
When the arrows loop round, no order can promise that everything read is already computed. The answer is to scan in rounds: cells not reached yet read “—” or what the last round left, and every round brings the answers a step closer to the truth. During a run, yellow frames mark the cells that changed this round.

When a round changes nothing, it stops: every cell now satisfies its own rule, which is called a fixed point, and repeating until nothing changes is called iterating to convergence. If the rule keeps making the numbers bigger and never settles, the machine tells you the table never settles.
Improving shortest-route answers round after round like this is the Bellman-Ford algorithm. Routers on a network swapping notes on “how far it is to everywhere” work the same way.
state-graph/glossary.entries.forward.bod: Viterbi only wants the single best explanation. To count in every explanation and ask how likely the sentence is altogether, use the forward algorithm.
The shape of the table and every cell’s ways in are the same as in Viterbi; only a few components change. The same skeleton answers yet another question.
A cell need not hold a number; it can hold “yes / no” and answer “can it be done?” questions. Games where two players take turns fill a table this way too: each cell is a position, holding “can the player whose turn it is win?”.

Once you move, your opponent faces the new position. So whether a position wins depends on which positions you can send your opponent into. A position the player to move can always win is a winning position; one where every move loses is a losing position.
state-graph/glossary.entries.games.title: Winning and losing positions
state-graph/glossary.entries.greedy.body: Picking whatever looks best right now at every step is called greedy, like packing a backpack “most valuable first” or “best value per kilo first”.

Greedy is quick and simple, but it does not always give the best result: the step that looks best now can block a better combination later. Dynamic programming compares every possibility in its table, so nothing is missed.
state-graph/glossary.entries.interval.bo: In some problems the subproblems are stretches of the original string: from item i to item j. Lay them out as an interval table, where cell (i, j) holds that stretch’s answer; only half the table is used, since a stretch always starts before it ends.
Every stretch is worked out from shorter stretches: drop one end, or drop both. So as long as shorter stretches are done first, the table can be filled.
The longest palindromic subsequence and the best order to multiply a chain of matrices: they are both interval tables.
state-graph/glossary.entries.knap01.body: A backpack has a weight limit, every item has a weight and a value, and each item can be taken at most once: how do you pack the most value? This is the 0/1 knapsack: each item is taken 0 times or 1 time.

In the knapsack table the rows are items and the columns are capacities: a cell holds “the most value you can pack choosing only from the first few items, with this much room”. Look only at the last item, and it has just two fates: taken, or left.
Choosing courses, setting a budget, loading a container, handing out jobs to servers: it is behind all of them.
state-graph/glossary.entries.layers.body: If the state forgets something, make it remember one more thing: copy the table into several layers, one per situation. This is called adding a dimension to the state.
Then lay down how to move between layers. A set of situations plus the rules for switching between them is called a state machine.
state-graph/glossary.entries.lcs.body.0: A string of letters that appears in order in both of two strings, with letters skipped in between allowed, is a common subsequence. The longest one is the longest common subsequence.
state-graph/glossary.entries.lcs.body.1: Finding what changed between two files, comparing how alike two stretches of DNA are, telling whether one part of homework was copied from another: they all use it.
state-graph/glossary.entries.lcs.title: Longest common subsequence
state-graph/glossary.entries.lis.body.0: From a row of numbers, pick some from left to right, each bigger than the last, skipping any you like: how many can you pick? This is the longest increasing subsequence.
state-graph/glossary.entries.lis.body.1: The key is the state: each cell holds the answer “ending with this one”, and the answer for the whole row is the largest of them. How many days in a run of share prices can be picked, each higher than the one before, is the same problem.
state-graph/glossary.entries.lis.title: Longest increasing subsequence
Two long stretches of DNA may not be alike overall, yet hide a short part that is very alike. Comparing from end to end is global alignment (the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm); looking only for the most alike part is local alignment (the Smith-Waterman algorithm).
The key step in local alignment: once a score drops below 0 it is cut to 0, starting afresh from there. So the most alike part can be anywhere in the table, and the answer is the largest cell in it.
Biologists searching gene databases for similar parts use exactly this.
state-graph/glossary.entries.local.title: Local Alignment
state-graph/glossary.entries.manyWays.bo: In some tables a cell has a fixed few ways in; in other problems the ways in are a whole run of earlier cells, and how many depends on the data.
The simplest example is the prefix sum: how much there is in all from the start up to here.
As long as the ways in are all earlier and already computed, the table can be filled however many there are and however they vary.
state-graph/glossary.entries.memo.body.0: Ask top-down, but write down every answer you get and look it up the next time it is asked: this is called memoisation, or memoised recursion. That way each cell is really worked out only once.
state-graph/glossary.entries.memo.body.1: Bottom-up filling and memoised recursion walk the same dependency graph, just in different ways: one settles the order and then fills in, the other works things out as it asks.
state-graph/glossary.entries.memo.title: Memoisation
state-graph/glossary.entries.memory.body: In some levels the table is stacked in several layers: besides “which cell”, the state remembers other things too, such as which keys are in hand. Every extra thing remembered doubles the layers.
Layercake works once on the same cell of every layer, and every layer shares the same circuit board; the This cell panel tells it how things stand on that layer.
Remember too little and the answers go wrong; remember too much and the table explodes. A good state is just enough: it remembers only what affects the future.
state-graph/glossary.entries.overlap.bod: Ask your way down: to know how many ways lead to step n, ask step n − 1 and step n − 2, which ask further down in turn… and the same small question gets asked again and again. These are overlapping subproblems.
The fix is simple: write down every answer you work out, and next time just look it up instead of working it out again. That is why filling the table computes each cell only once.
The same string of words means different things depending on how it is merged, two at a time, into phrases. Draw the merging and you get a parse tree.

How many ways a string of words can be merged is worked out in an interval table again: the last merge joins a left part and a right part at some split point. These counts are the Catalan numbers, which shoot up as the words grow in number.
Real parsing uses the CKY algorithm (also written CYK), which also checks grammar rules: which two parts can merge, and into what. The table has exactly the same shape.
state-graph/glossary.entries.parse.title: Parsing
state-graph/glossary.entries.policy.body: Once the values are known, choosing a move is easy: always step to the neighbour with the highest value. Taken together, “what to do here” for every cell is called a policy.
Each cell looks only at its own neighbours, yet together they make a complete map for finding the way. Judge the values first, then follow them, and the policy grows by itself.
state-graph/glossary.entries.recognise.b: Real problems never say on them. Faced with a new one, start with three questions: how many possibilities are there for the last step? Can the answers to small problems build the big one? What must the state remember?
Some problems do not need it at all: if there are no smaller problems to break off and build back up, simply looking through from start to finish is enough.
The rule for working out a cell from other cells is called the transition; written as a formula it is a recurrence, such as “this crossing = up + left”.

The trusty way to find the rule is to look only at the last step: just before arriving here, where could the last step have come from? Each possibility matches a cell that has already been worked out, and you combine them.
In the game, the circuit board is the transition: written once, and followed by the robot on every cell.
state-graph/glossary.entries.rolling.bod: If each row only uses the row above it, there is no need to keep the whole table: keep a single row and rewrite it in place. This is a <part-ref to="state-graph/roll"></part-ref>, and it can squash a table of thousands of rows into one.

Rewriting in place has a catch: the cell you read while rewriting another may already have been rewritten in this pass, and then it holds a value where this item has already been taken. The direction you rewrite in decides whether you read the old value or the new one.
A backpack where each item can be taken many times is the unbounded knapsack. The same circuit board, with only the rewrite direction changed, switches between the two kinds.
state-graph/glossary.entries.rolling.tit: Rolling arrays and the unbounded knapsack
state-graph/glossary.entries.seam.body.0: To make a picture narrower without squashing what is in it, find a seam running from top to bottom, one pixel per row, and cut it out.
state-graph/glossary.entries.seam.body.1: Every pixel has an energy: the more it differs from its neighbours, the higher it is, as on the edges of letters. The seam with the least energy is a cheapest route, found the same way as any cheapest route, only heading in a different direction.
state-graph/glossary.entries.seam.body.2: Cut one seam, work it out again, cut the next: this is content-aware resizing. Photo editors use it to turn a wide photo into a tall one.
state-graph/glossary.entries.seam.title: Seam carving
With the asking method, every extra step multiplies the number of questions by a fixed factor. Growth that snowballs like this is exponential: add a few more steps and the asking never finishes.
Filling the table takes about as many computations as the table has cells: one more step is just one more cell. Growth like n or n² as the problem gets bigger is called polynomial time.
Dynamic programming is fast not because any one step is clever, but because nothing is repeated: an exponential number of routes is squeezed into a polynomial number of cells.
state-graph/glossary.entries.speed.title: Exponential and polynomial
state-graph/glossary.entries.stairs.body: Climbing 1 or 2 steps at a time, how many ways are there to reach step n? It is the most common first problem in dynamic programming.

On the surface it has nothing to do with counting routes. But look only at the last step and a familiar structure appears: each cell’s answer comes from a few earlier cells, plus a start. Spot the same structure and an old part can be used as it is.
The situation a cell of the table stands for is called a state, such as “standing at this crossing” or “having seen the first few houses”. The number in the cell is that state’s answer.
A good state remembers everything that affects the future. If two different histories land in the same cell but can go on to do different things, that cell cannot keep an accurate answer.
Designing the state is the hardest and most important step in dynamic programming: only once you know what each cell holds can you write its rule.
state-graph/glossary.entries.state.title: State
state-graph/glossary.entries.stateSize.b: The machine computes once per cell, however many cells the table has. Multiply the sizes of the state’s dimensions and you get the number of cells: two words, for instance, give an alignment table of roughly one length times the other cells.

Each extra yes-or-no thing remembered doubles the layers: remember k things and there are 2 to the power k layers. Remembering more feels safer, but the table keeps growing; this is called state explosion.
So a good state is just enough: it leaves out nothing that affects the future, and remembers nothing that does not.
state-graph/glossary.entries.topdown.bod: Settling an order first and filling in cell by cell, from small problems up to the big one, is called bottom-up. Every table up to this point was filled in that way.

The other way round, starting from the big question and asking whichever cells it needs, is called top-down; in a program it is recursion. It needs no order worked out in advance, but unless the answers are written down, the same question gets asked many times.
state-graph/glossary.entries.topo.body.0: The machine works through the cells in some computing order. The cells a cell reads must be ready first, so a legal order has just one requirement: every cell comes after the cells it reads. An order that meets it is called a topological order.
state-graph/glossary.entries.topo.body.1: The order and the circuit go together: the circuit decides which cells each cell reads, and so which orders are legal; change the order, and the cells the circuit can read change with it.
state-graph/glossary.entries.topo.title: Computing order and topological order
state-graph/glossary.entries.valueIter.b: On a map with rewards and penalties, ask “how good is it to stand on each cell?”. A cell’s value depends on how good the neighbours it can reach are, with a discount for every step further away.

A rule like “value = the best result one step away, discounted” is called the Bellman equation. Start with every cell at 0 and scan round after round until nothing changes, and you have every cell’s value: this is value iteration.
It is one of the oldest foundations of reinforcement learning: game-playing programs and robots learning to walk all have to learn to judge “how good is it to be here?”.
state-graph/glossary.entries.viterbi.bod: Which part of speech is each word in a sentence? Put the words in columns and the parts of speech in rows; each cell holds “the cheapest explanation so far, with the earlier words tagged and this word tagged this way”.
Each column only looks at the one before it. The best cell in the last column is the best tagging of the whole sentence, and backtracking reads off each word’s tag. This is the Viterbi algorithm.
Speech recognition turning sound into words, and keyboard apps turning pinyin into characters, use tables like this: one column per moment, one row per possibility.
state-graph/glossary.entries.wordBreak.b: Can a string of letters with no spaces be split into words from a dictionary? Cell i holds “can the first i letters be split?”, as a “yes / no”.

Look only at the last word: it starts at some earlier position and ends here. A search engine facing a web address with no spaces, or a keyboard app facing a long run of pinyin, has to split it like this first.

state-graph/level.arrows.debrief.body.0: Each cell looks only at its own neighbours, yet together they make a complete navigation map: start anywhere, follow the arrows, and you will skirt the walls and traps and reach the treasure.
state-graph/level.arrows.debrief.body.1: In reinforcement learning these arrows are called a : in a given state, which action to take. Estimate the values first, then follow them, and the policy grows by itself.
state-graph/level.arrows.debrief.note: Policy = from every cell, head for the neighbour with the largest value.
state-graph/level.arrows.debrief.title: The value table is a satnav
state-graph/level.arrows.intro.0.t: The values are worked out. Now, which way to go? Simple: at every step, move to the neighbour with the largest value.
state-graph/level.arrows.intro.1.t: This level has three starting points. From each one, you choose the robot’s moves step by step.
state-graph/level.arrows.intro.2.t: Once all three are done, see what grows across the whole map.
state-graph/level.arrows.mission.goal: On a map whose values are already worked out, walk from each of the three starting points to the treasure. Every step must go to the neighbour with the largest value.
state-graph/level.arrows.mission.how: Click a neighbour in a dashed frame and the robot moves there.
state-graph/level.arrows.title: The arrows grow by themselves
state-graph/level.breach.debrief.body.0: The two routes stop on the same cell, so a counter that remembers only position stores them in the same cell. Yet one carries the key and the other is empty-handed: on the next step, one can go through the door and the other can’t.
state-graph/level.breach.debrief.body.1: Same state, different futures: that is hard proof the state design has a hole in it.
state-graph/level.breach.debrief.body.2: You already know how to fix it: make the state remember one more thing.
state-graph/level.breach.debrief.note: Counterexample: two histories that land in the same state but have different futures.
state-graph/level.breach.debrief.title: You found a counterexample
state-graph/level.breach.intro.0.t: A maze where you can only go right or down. One cell holds a key, and some cells are doors: only someone who has picked up the key can pass through a door.
state-graph/level.breach.intro.1.t: Your old friend the has been sent in to count the routes. But its state remembers only one thing: which cell you are on.
state-graph/level.breach.intro.2.t: When two routes reach the same cell, one with the key and one without, the counter stores them in the same cell. But their futures differ: when a door lies ahead, one can get through and the other can’t.
state-graph/level.breach.intro.3.t: Two histories with “the same state but different futures” are called a <wiki-ref to="state-graph/counterexample"></wiki-ref>. In <level-ref to="state-graph/robber"></level-ref>, the machine found one for you. This level, you find one yourself, proving that remembering only the position isn’t enough.
state-graph/level.breach.mission.goal: Draw two routes that only go right or down and stop on the same cell, one with the key and one without, with a door just ahead. That proves a counter that remembers only position gets it wrong.
state-graph/level.breach.mission.how: Choose route A or B in the side panel and click cells starting from the start, going only right or down. Click a route’s last cell to undo. When you are done, click “Check”.
state-graph/level.breach.short: This time you find the counterexample
state-graph/level.breach.tasks.breach.hi: The key is at the left end of row 2. Send one route down first to get the key and the other right first, then have them meet just left of or above a door.
state-graph/level.breach.title: Find the flaw
state-graph/level.brokenstairs.debrief.b: A broken step holds “—”. The steps above skip it when they add up, so the ways through it simply drop out.
<level-ref to="state-graph/rocks"></level-ref> did the same thing in the grid city: parts care about structure, not whether they count crossings or steps.
state-graph/level.brokenstairs.intro.0.t: A few steps on this staircase are broken and can’t be stepped on; they are drawn like rocks. Each stride still goes up 1 or 2 steps.
state-graph/level.brokenstairs.mission.g: Each stride goes up 1 or 2 steps, never onto a broken step. Work out how many ways there are to reach the top step.
state-graph/level.brokenstairs.mission.h: Work up from the ground, one step at a time.
state-graph/level.brokenstairs.short: The route counter behind a gate
state-graph/level.brokenstairs.tasks.bro: Some steps are broken and can’t be stepped on. Read “is broken”.
The <part-ref to="state-graph/counter"></part-ref> in your components box counts ways too: 1 step down and 2 steps down are its two ways in, and the ground is its start.
Cut off the broken steps: a Block gate outputs “—” when its condition is “yes”.
state-graph/level.brokenstairs.title: Broken stairs
state-graph/level.carve.debrief.body.0: The picture is 8 columns narrower, and neither letter is distorted at all: every seam slipped through unremarkable background. Squash the picture instead, and every letter gets squeezed thin.
state-graph/level.carve.debrief.body.1: This is called content-aware resizing (seam carving). When photo-editing software turns a landscape photo into a portrait one, this is how: a seam table, plus one trace back.
state-graph/level.carve.debrief.body.2: The edges you computed in Vision Complete became the robot’s terrain here. The two games share more than code underneath: they share ideas.
state-graph/level.carve.debrief.note: Seam carving: trace back from the smallest cell in the seam table’s bottom row, cut that seam out, and the picture is one column narrower.
state-graph/level.carve.debrief.title: Content-aware resizing
state-graph/level.carve.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="state-graph/seam"></level-ref> you worked out the seam table. This level you actually cut seams out.
state-graph/level.carve.intro.1.t: You find the first seam: click the smallest cell in the bottom row, then trace back up row by row. Of the three candidates on the row above, which one did the seam come from?
state-graph/level.carve.intro.2.t: Once a seam is cut, the picture is a column narrower, and the energy and seam table have to be worked out again. Leave the remaining seams to the machine, 8 in all. At the end, compare the result with simply squashing the picture.
state-graph/level.carve.mission.goal: Find the lowest-energy seam and cut it out. Cut 8 seams in all, making the picture 8 columns narrower.
state-graph/level.carve.mission.how: Trace the first seam back yourself: click the smallest cell in the bottom row, then click your way up row by row. The machine can cut the rest.
state-graph/level.carve.title: Cut it out
state-graph/level.change.debrief.body.0: The sweep arm steps back by each kind of coin, because the last coin can be any kind. For the fewest coins, take the min and + 1; to count the ways to pay, add them up.
state-graph/level.change.debrief.body.1: Look at the answers to the second question: 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 were counted as two ways. The table records only “how much has been made”, not which coins were used, so the order you pay in makes a different way. To count combinations only, you would have to bring the coins in one kind at a time, like .
state-graph/level.change.debrief.note: Making change: the last coin can be any kind, so the ways in are one step back by each kind of coin.
state-graph/level.change.debrief.title: The coin problem
state-graph/level.change.intro.0.t: With 1, 2 and 5 yuan coins, how do you make 7 yuan with the fewest coins? And how many ways are there to pay it?
state-graph/level.change.intro.1.t: Cell i holds the answer for making i yuan.
state-graph/level.change.intro.2.t: This level’s sweep arm sweeps by stepping back one coin of each kind: as many kinds of coin, as many cells it sends. Stepping back below 0 yuan lands “out”.
state-graph/level.change.mission.goal: Make each amount from the given coins. First work out the fewest coins needed, then how many ways there are to pay (paying the coins in a different order counts as a different way). An amount that can’t be made is “—”.
state-graph/level.change.mission.how: This level has two tasks, and the circuit board carries over to the second.
state-graph/level.change.short: Step back by each kind of coin
How many ways are there to pay? Paying the coins in a different order counts as a different way.
The last coin can be any kind, and each kind counts.
0 yuan counts as one way to pay (paying nothing): let a 1 through on “is 0 yuan”. No + 1 this time.
state-graph/level.change.tasks.change.as: What is the fewest coins needed?
state-graph/level.change.tasks.change.do: Same table, a different question: how many ways are there to pay? Think about which component to swap.
state-graph/level.change.tasks.change.hi: The last coin can be any kind: click the sweep arm, which sends the cells from before paying it (one coin of each kind stepped back).
An Adder can + 1 to every number in a whole run (counting this last coin), then wire it into “min”.
0 yuan needs no coins: let a 0 through on “is 0 yuan”.
state-graph/level.change.title: Making change
First “min” picks the cheaper of the two sides, then the cell’s own energy is added. And the machine went from “count how many routes there are” to “find the best route”.
Dynamic programming can count, and it can optimize. Both share the same skeleton: look only at the last step, and compute this cell from the answers of earlier cells.
state-graph/level.cheapest.debrief.note: To optimize, use “min” in place of “sum”.
state-graph/level.cheapest.debrief.title: From counting to optimizing
state-graph/level.cheapest.intro.0.t: Now every crossing costs some energy to pass through: the small number in each cell’s top-left corner. Going from the top left to the bottom right, what is the least energy you can spend?
state-graph/level.cheapest.intro.1.t: Again, look only at the last step: you reach this crossing either from above or from the left.
state-graph/level.cheapest.intro.2.t: When counting routes we added both sides, because routes from both sides count. This time you walk just one route: what should happen to the two sides? The Merger also has a “min” operation: given 8 and 6, it outputs 6. Add this crossing’s own energy, 1, and you get 7.
state-graph/level.cheapest.mission.goal: Only right or down, and every crossing you pass through (start and end included) costs the energy written in its top-left corner. Work out the least energy needed to get from the top left to the bottom right.
state-graph/level.cheapest.mission.how: The small number in a cell’s top-left corner is its energy; click “cell energy” in the inputs window to read it.
state-graph/level.cheapest.tasks.cheapes: You walk only one route, so the costs of the two sides can’t be added together. Use the “min” Merger.
You walk only one route: do both sides’ costs really count towards this crossing?
Passing through this crossing costs energy too: after the min, “cell energy” still has to be added.
state-graph/level.cheapest.title: Least effort
state-graph/level.city.debrief.body.0: Look back at what you did: 12 crossings, and every one did the same thing: the number above + the number to the left.
state-graph/level.city.debrief.body.1: The order mattered too: you filled from the top left towards the bottom right, because a crossing can only be worked out once the crossings above and to its left are filled.
state-graph/level.city.debrief.body.2: Doing the same thing 12 times is boring, and with 100 crossings it would be hopeless by hand.
state-graph/level.city.debrief.note: In a grid city, each crossing = the crossing above + the crossing to the left.
state-graph/level.city.debrief.title: The bottom right is 10
state-graph/level.city.intro.0.t: This city’s streets form a grid. Every street is one-way: you can only go right or down.
state-graph/level.city.intro.1.t: Apart from the top row and the left column, every crossing has two arrows coming in: one from above and one from the left.
state-graph/level.city.intro.2.t: Use the method from <level-ref to="state-graph/lastStep"></level-ref> to fill in the number of routes to every crossing. The start in the top-left corner already holds 1.
state-graph/level.city.mission.goal: Fill in the number of routes to every crossing. Streets only go right or down; the start in the top-left corner counts as 1, and the bottom-right corner gives the total.
state-graph/level.city.mission.how: Click a crossing and type its number on the keypad.
state-graph/level.city.short: Every crossing does the same thing
state-graph/level.city.title: Grid city
Going one coin to a row, every way is counted once: it grows on the rows of the coins it uses, so a different order is never counted again.
state-graph/level.coinways.debrief.title: One coin to a row
state-graph/level.coinways.intro.0.t: How many ways are there to make 5 yuan from 1-, 2- and 5-yuan coins? There are as many of each coin as you like, and only which coins you use counts, not their order: 1 + 2 + 2 and 2 + 1 + 2 are the same way.
state-graph/level.coinways.intro.1.t: The table looks like the knapsack table: rows are coins, columns are amounts. Row 0, “no coins”, only makes 0 yuan, which counts as 1 way; it is filled in already.
state-graph/level.coinways.mission.goal: Work out how many ways there are to make the amount.
state-graph/level.coinways.mission.how: Row by row, left to right.
state-graph/level.coinways.tasks.coinway: This row’s ways split in two: no coin of this kind at all, or at least one.
With at least one: take one off, and what is left may still use this coin, so it stays on this row.
state-graph/level.coinways.title: How many ways to pay
state-graph/level.confluence.debrief.bod: Before, you filled in 12 crossings by hand; now you drew three wires and the robot filled in the whole city.
The 1 at the start was written in for the robot.
state-graph/level.confluence.debrief.not: A Merger adds up the numbers its wires bring; “—” is left out.
state-graph/level.confluence.intro.0.t: Back to the grid city: streets only go right or down, and routes to each crossing = up + left. This time the start in the top-left corner already holds a 1 for you, and the robot takes care of the other crossings.
state-graph/level.confluence.intro.1.t: A wire carries just one number. To add up and left together you need a component: the Merger. It has three input dots on top; it adds up whatever is wired in and sends the result out of the dot at its bottom.
state-graph/level.confluence.intro.2.t: For cells in the top row there is no cell above: the view shows “out”, and what comes in is “—”, meaning “there is no road here”. The Merger skips “—” and adds up only real numbers.
state-graph/level.confluence.intro.3.t: Placing a component: drag the Merger from the tray under the board onto an empty slot of the board (a click works too). Hold it to drag it to another slot; drag it back to the tray to remove it.
state-graph/level.confluence.mission.goa: Streets only go right or down, and the start already holds 1. Have the robot work out the number of routes to every crossing: each crossing = up + left.
state-graph/level.confluence.mission.how: Click the “up” and “left” cells in the view, place a Merger, wire both outputs of the View part into it, then wire the Merger to “this cell”.
state-graph/level.confluence.short: Merge two numbers in one component
state-graph/level.confluence.tasks.confl: Step 1: click “up” and “left” in the view: the “View” part then has two outputs.
Step 2: drag the <part-ref to="part:table/msum"></part-ref> from the tray onto an empty slot of the board, or just click it.
Step 3: wire each of the View’s two outputs into a dot on the Merger’s left, then wire the Merger’s right-hand dot to “this cell”.
Each crossing = up + left: wire both inputs into the same Merger, and the Merger into “this cell”.
state-graph/level.confluence.title: Two roads meet
The board didn’t change at all; only how the layers connect did. Stepping from “just sold” back to “empty-handed” is the day of rest.
<level-ref to="state-graph/stock1"></level-ref> is this one with an arrow cut: once sold, there is no going back.
state-graph/level.cooldown.debrief.title: The same board
state-graph/level.cooldown.intro.0.t: Now you may trade as often as you like, but not buy on the day after you sell: you have to rest a day.
state-graph/level.cooldown.intro.1.t: There are still three states: empty-handed, holding, just sold. “Just sold” turns back into “empty-handed” a day later, and that step brings in 0.
state-graph/level.cooldown.mission.goal: Work out the most money you can make.
state-graph/level.cooldown.mission.how: How the layers connect is set by the world. Does your board need to change?
state-graph/level.cooldown.title: A day’s rest
state-graph/level.copy.debrief.body.0: You drew a single wire, and the robot carried it out on every cell. The circuit board is the rule: you write it once, and the robot uses it on every cell.
state-graph/level.copy.debrief.note: A circuit board describes the rule for one cell; the robot runs it on every cell.
state-graph/level.copy.debrief.title: The robot learned to copy
state-graph/level.copy.intro.0.t: From this chapter on, the computing is done by a little robot. It walks through the whole table cell by cell and does the same thing on every cell.
state-graph/level.copy.intro.1.t: This level has a single row of cells, and the leftmost one already holds a number. The robot starts on cell 2 and walks right, and on each cell it copies the number from the cell to its left.
state-graph/level.copy.intro.2.t: How does the robot know to copy from the left? From the circuit board you wire up. The inputs pane shows the robot’s view: the red frame in the middle is the cell it stands on, where the result is written. The View part on the left of the circuit board is that view: click the “left” cell, and the part gains an output that brings that cell’s number into the circuit.
state-graph/level.copy.intro.3.t: Finally, drag a wire from the dot under the “left” input to “this cell”, the red-framed output at the bottom of the board. It means: whatever comes from the left, write it in this cell. You can also click one dot and then the other.
state-graph/level.copy.mission.goal: Have the robot copy the number in the leftmost cell, cell by cell, all the way to the right: every cell equals the cell to its left.
state-graph/level.copy.mission.how: Click the “left” cell in the view: the View part gets an output for it. Wire that to “this cell”, then click “Run tests”.
state-graph/level.copy.short: Click a cell, wire it in
state-graph/level.copy.tasks.copy.diagno: The robot walks from left to right, so when it reaches a cell, the cell to its right is still empty and can’t be read.
Step 1: click the “left” cell in the view, and the “View” part gains an output.
Step 2: drag a wire from the dot on the “View” part’s right to “this cell”.
Step 3: click “Run tests” and watch the robot copy its way along, cell by cell.
Click “left” in the view, then wire the new output on the “View” part to “this cell”.
state-graph/level.copy.title: Robot relay
state-graph/level.edit.debrief.body.0: The fewest steps that turn one word into another is called the edit distance. Autocorrect, a search engine’s “Did you mean…?” and the analysis of gene mutations all rely on it.
state-graph/level.edit.debrief.body.1: Compared with , the table’s shape didn’t change at all: you just gave every way in a cost and took the min. Even the row and column along the edges were computed by the same circuit. The same alignment table with a different circuit board answers a different question.
state-graph/level.edit.debrief.note: Edit distance: delete, insert and replace each cost 1, a matching letter can be kept for free, and you take the min.
state-graph/level.edit.debrief.title: Edit distance
state-graph/level.edit.intro.0.t: only allowed swapping letters. But typing also adds and drops letters, so real correction has to answer: what is the fewest steps that turn one word into another?
state-graph/level.edit.intro.1.t: Each step does exactly one thing: delete a letter, insert a letter, or replace one letter with another. For example, CAT → CUT takes just 1 step: replace A with U.
state-graph/level.edit.intro.2.t: It’s an alignment table again: the rows are the original word, the columns the target word. Each cell records the fewest steps that turn “the first few letters of the original” into “the first few letters of the target”. Each of the three neighbors has a meaning:
state-graph/level.edit.intro.3.t: Every way in has its own cost: how many extra steps it takes to come that way. Deleting, inserting and replacing each cost 1 step; when the two letters match, coming from the up-left lets you keep the letter for free.
state-graph/level.edit.intro.4.t: This time, row 0 and column 0 have no ready-made numbers; the circuit has to compute them too. Think: how many steps turn the first 3 letters of the original into an empty word? And when both words are empty?
state-graph/level.edit.mission.goal: Each step deletes, inserts or replaces one letter. Build the typo-fixing circuit and work out the fewest steps that turn one word into another.
state-graph/level.edit.mission.how: This board needs quite a few components. Once you pass, look at the exact edits the table traces back.
state-graph/level.edit.short: Every way in has a cost
Deleting a letter (from above), inserting one (from the left) and replacing one (from the up-left) each cost 1 more step. To get the fewest steps, how should these three ways in be combined?
When the two letters match you can just keep it: come from the up-left at no cost. Use a Pass gate with “letters match” as its condition and “up-left” as its number.
The start (both words empty) is 0 steps: let a 0 through on “is start”. Finally, wire all three paths into another “min” Merger.
state-graph/level.edit.title: Fix the typo
state-graph/level.enough.debrief.body.0: The green key has no door; the blue door always comes after the blue key. These two things don’t affect the future, so there’s no need to remember them. Remembering only the red key, 2 layers are enough.
state-graph/level.enough.debrief.title: Just enough
state-graph/level.enough.intro.0.t: Three keys again. But this level’s state remembers only the red key, so the table has just 2 layers.
state-graph/level.enough.mission.goal: Work out the number of valid routes, and see whether remembering one key is enough.
state-graph/level.enough.mission.how: Every cell works out both layers.
state-graph/level.enough.short: Remember only what affects the future
state-graph/level.enough.title: Just enough?
state-graph/level.forward.debrief.body.0: Same table, same skeleton: Viterbi is “min and add”, this is “sum and multiply”. The first finds the best tagging; the second counts them all.
state-graph/level.forward.debrief.body.1: This is the forward algorithm. When speech recognition compares “which sentence does this sound most resemble”, this is how it works out the probability of each sentence.
state-graph/level.forward.debrief.note: Forward algorithm: Viterbi’s “min and add” becomes “sum and multiply”.
state-graph/level.forward.debrief.title: The forward algorithm
state-graph/level.forward.intro.0.t: A different question: not “which tagging is best”, but “counting every tagging, how likely is this sentence to appear”.
state-graph/level.forward.intro.1.t: Costs become probabilities (numbers between 0 and 1): the probability of one tagging is every probability along the way multiplied together; the probability of the sentence is all the taggings added up. “Start” holds 1.
state-graph/level.forward.intro.2.t: Compare with <level-ref to="state-graph/tagging"></level-ref>: there you wanted only the best tagging; here every tagging counts, and the parts of a tagging are multiplied this time. Which components in the circuit need swapping? When counting routes, you added up every route.
state-graph/level.forward.intro.3.t: The little bar under a cell shows its share of its column: the longer the bar, the more likely this word is to be this part of speech.
state-graph/level.forward.mission.goal: Work out how likely the sentence is: the sum of the probabilities of every tagging. Each tagging’s probability is the “after …” and “this word, this tag” probabilities along the way, multiplied together.
state-graph/level.forward.mission.how: The circuit’s skeleton is the same as <level-ref to="state-graph/tagging"></level-ref>’s: think about which components need swapping.
state-graph/level.forward.short: Min becomes sum, add becomes multiply
This time you don’t pick the best one: every tagging counts, so use “sum”.
Start from <level-ref to="state-graph/tagging"></level-ref>’s circuit: which component joins the parts of one tagging, and which one chooses among the possibilities?
Add the three together, then multiply by the “this word, this tag” probability.
state-graph/level.forward.title: How likely is this sentence
state-graph/level.frog.debrief.body.0: The view only sees what is nearby. The arm lets a cell read a cell however far away, and how far is decided by the number written on the cell itself.
state-graph/level.frog.debrief.title: Reaching however far
state-graph/level.frog.intro.0.t: A frog wants to cross a river. There is a row of stones, and the bank counts as stone 0. Each stone says “↶ k”: the frog can only jump onto it from the stone k back.
state-graph/level.frog.intro.1.t: The stone k back can be far away, out of a 5×5 view. This era’s robot, Longarm, has a <wiki-ref to="table/arms"></wiki-ref>: on each stone it reaches the stone k back. What the arm reaches sits under the view; click it and the View part gets an output for it.
state-graph/level.frog.mission.goal: Work out how many jumps the frog needs to reach the last stone.
state-graph/level.frog.mission.how: Work forward from the bank, stone by stone. On the bank the frog hasn’t jumped yet: 0 jumps.
state-graph/level.frog.tasks.frog.diagno: The frog jumps from the stone k back, and that stone is read with the arm.
Before this jump the frog was on the stone the arm reaches: its count + 1.
On the bank there are no jumps yet: let a 0 through a Pass gate.
state-graph/level.frog.title: The frog crosses
state-graph/level.frogfar.debrief.body.0: It is climbing stairs, with “2 steps down” swapped for the stone the arm reads. A way in can be any distance away; the structure stays the same.
state-graph/level.frogfar.debrief.title: Climbing stairs again
state-graph/level.frogfar.intro.0.t: The frog in this river is more agile: it can jump on from the stone before, or from the stone marked “↶ k”. A stone with no ↶ can only be reached from the one before.
state-graph/level.frogfar.mission.goal: Work out how many different ways the frog can get from the bank to the last stone.
state-graph/level.frogfar.mission.how: The bank counts as 1 way: the frog is already there.
state-graph/level.frogfar.short: The view and the arm together
The frog can also come from the stone before, which is in the view.
Where the long jump comes from is read with the arm.
Where does the last jump come from? The stone before, or the one the arm reaches. Count both: add them up.
The bank counts as 1 way: let a 1 through a Pass gate.
state-graph/level.frogfar.title: A longer leap
state-graph/level.ice.debrief.body.0: This board reads each cell’s own chances. With 0 everywhere it is <level-ref to="state-graph/treasure"></level-ref>; with the same chance everywhere it is <level-ref to="state-graph/slip"></level-ref>.
state-graph/level.ice.debrief.body.1: Real reinforcement learning works the same way: the uncertainty differs from state to state, and each value is weighted by that state’s own chances.
state-graph/level.ice.debrief.title: One board, three maps
state-graph/level.ice.intro.0.t: Some cells on this map are ice and some are ground. Ground doesn’t slip; each cell of ice slips its own way, with its chance written in the corner.
state-graph/level.ice.intro.1.t: This cell’s facts include its chance to slip and its chance to hold (they add up to 1). Going right = hold × right + slip × down; going down is the other way round.
state-graph/level.ice.mission.goal: Work out every cell’s value: the better of the two moves × 0.9, each move weighted by this cell’s chance to slip.
state-graph/level.ice.mission.how: The chance to slip changes from cell to cell: read it from the cell’s facts, not from a Constant.
state-graph/level.ice.short: Every cell slips its own way
state-graph/level.ice.tasks.ice.diagnose: Every cell slips its own way: read both chances from the cell’s facts.
state-graph/level.ice.tasks.ice.hints.0: As in <level-ref to="state-graph/slip"></level-ref>, with 0.8 and 0.2 swapped for this cell’s “chance to hold” and “chance to slip”.
state-graph/level.ice.title: Ice and ground
state-graph/level.keydoor.debrief.body.0: Routes on the “no keys” layer stop at a door; reaching the key cell, they move as a batch to the “red” layer. The “red” layer takes them in at the key cell, and from then on every door is open.
state-graph/level.keydoor.debrief.body.1: The state went from “which cell” to “which cell, and whether you have the key”: one more thing to remember, one more layer.
state-graph/level.keydoor.debrief.title: Two layers, each minding its own
state-graph/level.keydoor.intro.0.t: To fix the counter, the state has to remember one more thing: whether you have the key. Each cell of one table can hold only one number, which can’t keep two kinds of route apart.
state-graph/level.keydoor.intro.1.t: This level’s robot, Layercake, stacks the table in two layers: the “no keys” layer holds the routes that haven’t got the key yet, the “red” layer those that have. On every cell it works out both layers.
state-graph/level.keydoor.intro.2.t: The cell facts tell the circuit what happens on this layer at this cell. Door shut: there is a door here, but this layer has no key. Routes move on: there is a key here, and routes reaching it pick it up and move to the other layer. Picks up key: there is a key here, and this layer takes in the routes that pick it up.
state-graph/level.keydoor.intro.3.t: On the cell with the key, Layercake’s probe reaches up and left on the other layer: that is where those routes come from.
state-graph/level.keydoor.mission.goal: Only right or down, and you must have picked up the key before going through a door. Work out the number of valid routes on each map: the end cells of both layers, added up.
state-graph/level.keydoor.mission.how: Every cell works out both layers.
state-graph/level.keydoor.short: Stack the table in two layers
Count the routes with the Route Counter first, then block the ones that can’t stay on this layer: the door is shut, or the routes move on.
On the cell where the key is picked up, also take in the routes moving over from the other layer: up and left as the probe reaches them, added up.
state-graph/level.keydoor.title: Keys and doors
Make room on this row: this row has already considered this kind, so taking one more from there is simply one more of it.
It differs from the 0/1 knapsack in one place only: the cell that makes room moves from the row above to this row. This problem is called the unbounded knapsack (unlimited copies of each item).
state-graph/level.knapmany.debrief.title: Unbounded knapsack
state-graph/level.knapmany.intro.0.t: This time you pack in a shop: there is plenty of every kind of thing, and you can take several of the same kind. The total weight still can’t exceed the backpack’s capacity.
state-graph/level.knapmany.intro.1.t: The table is the same knapsack table: cell (row i, capacity w) records the most value you can pack choosing only from the first i kinds, with capacity w. Only one thing differs from : after taking one, you can take the same kind again.
state-graph/level.knapmany.intro.2.t: The telescopic arm still reaches as many columns to the left as this kind weighs, one cell on the row above and one on this row.
state-graph/level.knapmany.mission.goal: Each kind can be taken as many times as you like, and the total weight can’t exceed the capacity. Build the circuit board and work out the most value each backpack can hold.
state-graph/level.knapmany.mission.how: Still row by row, left to right.
state-graph/level.knapmany.tasks.knapman: Making room on the row above takes each kind only once. In this level, you can take several of the same kind.
Taking none of this kind: the answer is still right above.
After taking one, you may take another: you want the cell that has “already considered this kind”. The row above hasn’t considered it yet; this row has.
state-graph/level.knapmany.title: As many as you like
state-graph/level.knapmix.debrief.body.0: Each row looks at one kind only: if it can be taken at most once, make room on the row above; if many times, make room on this row.
state-graph/level.knapmix.debrief.body.1: The two earlier backpacks are special cases of it: everything at most once is the 0/1 knapsack, everything many times is the unbounded knapsack. This circuit board solves <level-ref to="state-graph/knapmany"></level-ref> as it is.
state-graph/level.knapmix.debrief.title: A mixed backpack
state-graph/level.knapmix.intro.0.t: Before setting off, you stock up at a shop. Some things come only once, like the tent or the camera; some come in any number, like water or biscuits. Items marked ×n can be taken many times.
state-graph/level.knapmix.intro.1.t: The cell facts now include “can take many”.
state-graph/level.knapmix.mission.goal: Each thing can be taken either at most once or as many times as you like, and the total weight can’t exceed the capacity. Work out the most value each backpack can hold.
state-graph/level.knapmix.mission.how: Items marked ×n can be taken many times.
In this level some things can be taken only once and some many times. Read “can take many”.
The two kinds of thing differ in one place only: whether the cell that makes room is on the row above or on this row.
Let “can take many” pick that cell: one gate lets this row’s cell through, another lets the row above’s through.
state-graph/level.knapmix.title: A mixed backpack
state-graph/level.knaptable.debrief.body: Each item has only two fates: left out (look right above), or taken (make room for its weight on the row above, then add its value). Take the larger of the two.
The way in must start from the row above. The row above hasn’t considered this item yet, so taking it from there guarantees it is taken only once.
This problem is called the <wiki-ref to="state-graph/knap01"></wiki-ref>. Choosing courses, budgeting, loading shipping containers and assigning jobs to servers all come down to it.
state-graph/level.knaptable.debrief.note: 0/1 knapsack: leave it out, look right above; take it, make room for its weight on the row above and add its value.
state-graph/level.knaptable.intro.0.t: Turn packing into a table too. Rows are items and columns are backpack capacities 0, 1, 2… Cell (row i, capacity w) records: the most value you can pack choosing only from the first i items, with a backpack of capacity w.
state-graph/level.knaptable.intro.1.t: Row 0 means “no items considered yet”, so it is all 0s, and the machine has already filled it in.
state-graph/level.knaptable.intro.2.t: Look only at the last item: item i is either left out or taken. If it is left out, the answer is the same as the cell right above.
state-graph/level.knaptable.intro.3.t: And if it is taken? The backpack first has to make room for it. Think: before making room, which cell of the table is the backpack? What do you gain by taking the item? And in the end, between taking and leaving it, which do you want?
state-graph/level.knaptable.intro.4.t: This level’s robot, Longarm, stands on (row i, capacity w). The cell right above is in its view, but the cell as many columns to the left as the item weighs may be far away, out of view. The <wiki-ref to="table/arms"></wiki-ref> from the frog’s river comes in again: this time it reaches left by “this item’s weight” cells and reads one cell on the row above and one on this row; click a cell it reaches, and the “View” part gains an output for it. The This cell panel holds this item’s “item value”.
state-graph/level.knaptable.mission.goal: The total weight can’t exceed the capacity, and each item can be taken at most once. Build the knapsack table’s circuit and work out the most value each backpack can hold.
state-graph/level.knaptable.mission.how: The first two tests are the backpacks you packed by hand in <level-ref to="state-graph/pack"></level-ref>. Once you pass, the green cells show the packing traced back from the table.
state-graph/level.knaptable.tasks.knapta: Cells on the same row have already considered this item, so taking it again from there takes it twice. To take this item, make room on the row above.
Any item can be left out: then the answer is just “right above”.
Taking this item: make room for its weight on the row above, then add its value. Wire both choices into a “max” Merger.
state-graph/level.knaptable.title: Knapsack table
You didn’t list a single route, yet you worked out that there are 6.

Each place’s number was computed from the numbers of the places before it: first solve the small problems (how many routes reach the nearby places), then build the big answer out of those (how many reach School).
This is the core idea of dynamic programming.
state-graph/level.lastStep.debrief.note: Routes to a place = the sum of the routes to all of its “previous stops”.
state-graph/level.lastStep.debrief.title: 6 routes in all
state-graph/level.lastStep.intro.0.t: The map has grown. Tracing routes one by one is slow and easy to get wrong, so let’s try something else: give each place a number meaning “how many routes lead here from Home”.
state-graph/level.lastStep.intro.1.t: Home itself counts as 1 route: you are already standing there, and that is the one and only way of “arriving”.
state-graph/level.lastStep.intro.2.t: To find how many routes reach “Square”, look only at the last step: the arrows into Square come from Books and Park. So every route to Square makes its last step either from Books or from Park.
state-graph/level.lastStep.intro.3.t: The routes “coming from Books” are exactly the routes to Books, each with one more step. So: routes to Square = routes to Books + routes to Park.
state-graph/level.lastStep.intro.4.t: Every place works the same way: the routes to it = the sum of the routes to every place with an arrow into it. Start at Home and fill the places in, one by one, along the arrows.
state-graph/level.lastStep.mission.goal: Work out how many routes lead from Home to each place, ending with the number for School. You can only go the way the arrows point, and Home itself counts as 1.
state-graph/level.lastStep.mission.how: Click a place and type its number on the keypad below. The selected place’s “previous stops” get a dashed yellow frame.
state-graph/level.lastStep.title: Just look at the last step
state-graph/level.lawn.debrief.body.0: A cell holds “the side of the biggest square whose bottom-right corner I am”. It is one more than the smallest of the cells above, to the left and up-left: if any of them is short, the square can’t grow.
state-graph/level.lawn.debrief.body.1: Under a tree it is 0: the “sum” merger skips the “—” and only the Constant 0 is left.
state-graph/level.lawn.debrief.body.2: The hard part was not the wiring but deciding what a cell should hold.
state-graph/level.lawn.debrief.title: What a cell holds
state-graph/level.lawn.intro.0.t: A field has a few trees on it. You want to lay a square lawn on the open ground, lined up with the cells, without covering a tree. How big can it be?
state-graph/level.lawn.intro.1.t: The field is ringed above and to the left by 0s, meaning outside the field. The answer is the square’s side.
state-graph/level.lawn.mission.goal: Work out the side of the biggest square lawn.
state-graph/level.lawn.mission.how: The answer is the largest number anywhere in the table.
The answer is the largest number in the table. What square should the number in each cell describe?
Let each cell answer one question only: how big can a square be whose bottom-right corner it is?
state-graph/level.lawn.title: The biggest square
state-graph/level.lcs.debrief.body.0: In an alignment table, every diagonal step is one line drawn. You can only step diagonally where the letters match, and the path always runs from the top left to the bottom right, so the lines never cross.
state-graph/level.lcs.debrief.body.1: 7 letters against 6 would take ages to try by hand; the table filled in just 56 cells. Two stretches of DNA ten thousand letters long need only a hundred million cells, which a computer fills in the blink of an eye.
state-graph/level.lcs.debrief.note: Alignment table: if the letters match, up-left + 1; if not, the larger of up and left.
state-graph/level.lcs.debrief.title: The table drew the lines for you
state-graph/level.lcs.intro.0.t: With more letters, it gets hard to try every way of drawing the lines. So we hand it to a new kind of table: the <part-ref to="state-graph/align"></part-ref>. One word goes along the top, the other down the left.
state-graph/level.lcs.intro.1.t: Cell (row, column) records: the most lines you can draw between the first “row” letters of the left word and the first “column” letters of the top word. The bottom-right corner is the answer for the whole words.
state-graph/level.lcs.intro.2.t: Row 0 and column 0 mean “no letters at all”. An empty side can’t have any lines, so they are all 0, and the machine has already filled them in.
state-graph/level.lcs.intro.3.t: Once again, look only at the last step. Focus on the two last letters for the cell with the question mark: letter number “row” of the left word, and letter number “column” of the top word. There are only two cases: they are the same, or they are different.
state-graph/level.lcs.intro.4.t: Think through each case. When they are the same, can those two letters be linked by a line? Once they are, which cell of the table matches the letters that remain? When they are different, at least one of the two can’t get a line; drop it, and which cell matches then? The answers are all in the three cells next to the question mark, which are already computed.
state-graph/level.lcs.intro.5.t: The robot walks the alignment table cell by cell, and its view shows the cells up-left, up and left of it (a cell marked = is one where the row’s letter and the column’s letter match). In the This cell panel, “letters match” tells you whether the red frame’s row letter and column letter are the same. Work out which cell each case should read, then build the board.
state-graph/level.lcs.mission.goal: Build the alignment table’s circuit and work out the length of the longest common subsequence of two words (letters that appear in order in both).
state-graph/level.lcs.mission.how: The first two tests are the two puzzles you solved by hand in <level-ref to="state-graph/link"></level-ref>. Once you pass, look at the lines hidden in the table.
state-graph/level.lcs.short: Let the table draw the lines
state-graph/level.lcs.tasks.lcs.hints.0: When the letters match, those two can be linked by a line. Once they are, which neighbour of the question mark matches the letters that remain? Take that way only when they match: use a Pass gate with “letters match” as its condition.
state-graph/level.lcs.tasks.lcs.hints.1: When the letters differ, at least one of them gets no line: either drop this row’s letter (look up) or drop this column’s letter (look left).
state-graph/level.lcs.tasks.lcs.hints.2: To get the most lines: wire up, left and the Pass gate all into a “max” Merger.
state-graph/level.lcs.title: Alignment Table
state-graph/level.link.debrief.body.0: Read from left to right, the lines you drew spell out a sequence both strings share: a common subsequence. The most lines you can draw is the length of the .
state-graph/level.link.debrief.body.1: It has many uses: finding what changed between two versions of a file, measuring how alike two stretches of DNA are, telling whether one homework was copied from another.
state-graph/level.link.debrief.note: Common subsequence: letters that appear in order in both strings. The lines can’t cross.
state-graph/level.link.debrief.title: Longest common subsequence
state-graph/level.link.intro.0.t: A new chapter: comparing two strings. A sequence of letters that appears in order in both strings is called a common subsequence. In ABCD and ACBD, for example, A, B, D is one.
state-graph/level.link.intro.1.t: You can find a common subsequence by drawing lines: link a top letter to an equal bottom letter. There are three rules: only link equal letters; each letter takes at most one line; lines can’t cross.
state-graph/level.link.intro.2.t: Why can’t they cross? Crossing lines mean the two letters come in one order on top and the opposite order below, so reading them off wouldn’t give the same sequence.
state-graph/level.link.intro.3.t: The more lines, the longer the common subsequence. Your goal: draw as many lines as you can.
state-graph/level.link.mission.goal: In both puzzles, draw as many lines as possible. Only link equal letters, each letter takes at most one line, and lines can’t cross.
state-graph/level.link.mission.how: Click a letter, then the same letter in the other row, to draw a line. Click a letter that already has a line to remove it.
Leave C alone for now. C is first on top but third below, so linking it blocks both A and B.
The target is 4 lines. B, C, B, A is one way; B, D, A, B is another.
state-graph/level.link.title: Lines that never cross
state-graph/level.localalign.debrief.bod: Global alignment (comparing two strings end to end, the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm) uses the same scoring, differing only in “below 0 is cut to 0”: with that one change, the table goes from “how alike are they overall” to “where is the most alike stretch”. The cut needs no new component: take the max against 0.
This is the Smith-Waterman algorithm. Biologists use it to search gene databases for similar parts, and to check how closely a virus resembles known ones.
state-graph/level.localalign.debrief.not: Local alignment: below 0 is cut to 0; the answer is the largest cell in the table.
state-graph/level.localalign.intro.0.t: Two long stretches of DNA may not look alike overall, yet hide a short part in the middle that is very alike. How do you find it?
state-graph/level.localalign.intro.1.t: An alignment table again, with row 0 and column 0 all 0. Each step scores: a matching pair +2, a mismatched pair −1, and a gap (coming from up or left) −1. The “cell score” in the This cell panel is this cell’s pair: +2 or −1.
state-graph/level.localalign.intro.2.t: The key step: if a score comes out below 0, it is cut to 0, meaning “drop everything before and start again from here”. Starting afresh beats carrying a negative score along.
state-graph/level.localalign.intro.3.t: The most alike stretch isn’t necessarily in the bottom-right corner: it could be anywhere in the table, so the answer is the largest cell in the whole table.
state-graph/level.localalign.mission.goa: Find the most similar stretch of two strings: a match +2, a mismatch −1, a gap −1, and anything below 0 is cut to 0. The answer is the largest score in the table.
state-graph/level.localalign.mission.how: Constants can be set to negative numbers. Once you pass, see the stretch traced back from the table.
state-graph/level.localalign.tasks.local: Scores can go negative, and a negative score is worse than starting again: take the max once more, against a Constant 0.
Which step’s score does each of the three ways in add? To find the most alike stretch, how should they be combined?
Below 0 is cut to 0: add another “max”, with a Constant 0 in its other input.
state-graph/level.localalign.title: Find the most alike stretch
state-graph/level.loop.debrief.body.0: When routes can loop back, no order can promise that “everything read is already computed”. The way out is to scan again and again: every round brings the answers a step closer to the truth, and once a round changes nothing, you have it.
state-graph/level.loop.debrief.body.1: This is the Bellman-Ford algorithm. Routers on a network tell each other “how far it is to everywhere”, and find shortest paths with exactly this round-by-round “relaxing”.
state-graph/level.loop.debrief.note: With loops, one scan isn’t enough: scan round after round until the table stops changing.
state-graph/level.loop.debrief.title: Scan until it settles
state-graph/level.loop.intro.0.t: Every table so far has shared one unspoken rule: the arrows never loop back. The robot scans once in order, and every cell it reads is already computed.
state-graph/level.loop.intro.1.t: This city is different: you can move in all four directions, up, down, left and right, and entering each crossing costs the energy in its corner. The cheapest route may go right, then down, then left to loop back.
state-graph/level.loop.intro.2.t: Each cell reads four neighbours, but the cells below and to the right haven’t been reached yet this round. No matter: in this chapter the robot scans round after round. A cell not reached yet reads as “—”, or as whatever the last round left there; once a whole round changes nothing, it stops.
state-graph/level.loop.intro.3.t: While it runs, yellow frames mark the cells this round has changed. See how many rounds it takes.
state-graph/level.loop.mission.goal: You can move up, down, left or right, and entering each crossing costs the energy in its corner (the start counts too). Work out the least energy it takes to get from the top left to the bottom right.
state-graph/level.loop.mission.how: The robot scans round after round until the table stops changing. This level checks the whole table.
Any of the four directions can be a way in: wire up, down, left and right into “min”. A Merger has only three inputs, so chain two of them.
Finally add the cell energy. The start’s neighbours all begin as “—”, so use a Pass gate to let a 0 in at the start.
state-graph/level.loop.title: Going round
state-graph/level.lps.debrief.body.0: This board is nearly the one from <level-ref to="state-graph/lcs"></level-ref>: a max, plus a Pass gate that adds something when the letters match.
state-graph/level.lps.debrief.body.1: The alignment table compares two words; here you compare the two ends of one word. The table changed shape; the skeleton did not.
state-graph/level.lps.debrief.title: The same skeleton again
state-graph/level.lps.intro.0.t: Pick some letters out of a string, keeping their order but skipping any you like, so that what you picked reads the same forwards and backwards. How many can you pick at most? From CHARACTER, say, you can pick CARAC: 5 letters.
state-graph/level.lps.intro.1.t: The table is the one from <level-ref to="state-graph/palin"></level-ref>: the run from letter i to letter j has a cell, holding “the most letters you can pick from this run”. A single letter is a palindrome on its own, so the diagonal is already filled with 1.
state-graph/level.lps.mission.goal: Work out how many letters the longest palindrome you can pick from the whole string has.
state-graph/level.lps.tasks.lps.diagnose: When both ends are picked, what is left is the run without both ends: the cell down-left.
state-graph/level.lps.tasks.lps.hints.0: If the two end letters match, both can be picked. Which run is left to pick from, and which cell holds it?
state-graph/level.lps.tasks.lps.hints.1: If they differ, at least one end goes unused. Dropping the left end is the cell below, dropping the right end the cell to the left: take the larger.
state-graph/level.lps.title: The longest palindrome inside
It is the very same board as in <level-ref to="state-graph/cheapest"></level-ref>, with the merger swapped to “max” and energy swapped for gold.
state-graph/level.maxcoins.debrief.title: The same skeleton
state-graph/level.maxcoins.intro.0.t: Every crossing holds some gold coins: the number in each cell’s top-left corner. You may only go right or down, and you keep the coins at every crossing you pass through, start and end included.
state-graph/level.maxcoins.mission.goal: Going from the top left to the bottom right, how many coins can you collect at most?
state-graph/level.maxcoins.mission.how: Still row by row, from the top left.
state-graph/level.maxcoins.tasks.maxcoin: This time you want the most gold: use “max”.
You walk one route only: at this crossing, which side would you pick?
