The start has no way in, so the max gives “—”. At the start, feed a 0 into the merger.
state-graph/level.maxcoins.title: The richest route
state-graph/level.maxsub.debrief.body.0: A cell holds only “the best that ends today”: today alone, or joined to yesterday. The best run overall is the largest cell in the table.
state-graph/level.maxsub.debrief.body.1: Choose the right thing for a cell to hold, and the cell to the left is all you need.
state-graph/level.maxsub.debrief.title: No sweep arm needed
state-graph/level.maxsub.intro.0.t: A market stall’s daily takings: a profit is positive, a loss negative. Which run of consecutive days adds up to the most?
state-graph/level.maxsub.mission.goal: Work out the largest total of any run of consecutive days.
state-graph/level.maxsub.mission.how: The answer is the largest cell in the table.
state-graph/level.maxsub.tasks.maxsub.di: What the sweep arm adds up always starts on day 1, but the best run need not.
state-graph/level.maxsub.tasks.maxsub.hi: A cell need not hold “the best run up to today”. What else could it hold?
The best run ending today is either today alone, or the best run ending yesterday with today added.
state-graph/level.maxsub.title: The best stretch
state-graph/level.nim.debrief.body.0: For the “none left” cell you don’t need to wire anything: there is no move to make, “any yes” receives nothing, and it outputs “no”. A player with no move left loses.
state-graph/level.nim.debrief.body.1: Look at the row: no, yes, yes, no, yes, yes… every multiple of 3 loses. You never did any division: the pattern grew out of the table by itself.
state-graph/level.nim.debrief.note: In a game of taking turns: if any move drops the opponent into a “lose”, this cell is a “win”.
state-graph/level.nim.debrief.title: Winning and losing fill a table too
state-graph/level.nim.intro.0.t: There is a pile of stones on the table. Two players take turns, taking 1 or 2 stones each time, and whoever takes the last stone wins. You go first. Can you win?
state-graph/level.nim.intro.1.t: Lay out “how many are left” in a row, and let each cell record: with this many left and your turn to move, can you win? If it is your turn and none are left, your opponent has just taken the last stone: you have lost.
state-graph/level.nim.intro.2.t: Look only at your own move: take 1, and your opponent faces the “after taking 1” cell; take 2, and they face the “after taking 2” cell. Think: is the cell your opponent faces “yes” or “no” when you can win? Of the two ways to take, how many have to work?
state-graph/level.nim.intro.3.t: A new component, “Not”: “yes” becomes “no”, and “no” becomes “yes”. Each cell records “can the player to move win”. After you take your stones, whose move is it?
state-graph/level.nim.mission.goal: Take 1 or 2 stones each time; whoever takes the last stone wins. For each number of stones left, work out whether the player to move can win.
state-graph/level.nim.mission.how: This level checks the whole row. Click “after taking 1” and “after taking 2” in the view, and build the circuit.
state-graph/level.nim.tasks.nim.diagnose: After your move, whose turn is it? Each cell records “can the player to move win”, so your opponent’s “yes” is a “no” for you. Flip it with Not.
state-graph/level.nim.tasks.nim.hints.0: After your move, whose turn is it? If the opponent’s cell is “yes”, what does that mean for you?
state-graph/level.nim.tasks.nim.hints.1: Of the two ways to take, if either leaves the opponent losing, you win: wire both Nots into “any yes”.
state-graph/level.nim.title: Take the stones
state-graph/level.order.debrief.body.0: The machine works from the bottom right to the top left, so whenever a cell is computed, the cells to its right and below are already done. That is why the circuit can only read those two directions.
state-graph/level.order.debrief.body.1: The order and the circuit go together: compute the cells that others depend on before the cells that depend on them. Programmers call an order like that a “topological order”.
state-graph/level.order.debrief.body.2: The start cell’s answer is the same as before. Counting from the start to the end and counting back from the end to the start are two ways of asking the same question.
state-graph/level.order.debrief.note: A valid order: every cell comes after the cells it reads.
state-graph/level.order.debrief.title: The order decides what can be read
state-graph/level.order.intro.0.t: So far the machine has always started in the top-left corner and worked row by row. Why can’t it just start anywhere?
state-graph/level.order.intro.1.t: Because each cell reads the cells above it and to its left. If those are still empty, the machine can’t go on.
state-graph/level.order.intro.2.t: This level’s robot has been fitted backwards: it can only start from the bottom-right corner and walk the rows in reverse. The small number in each cell’s corner is the order in which it gets there.
state-graph/level.order.intro.3.t: The Route Counter reads up and left, but on this machine those cells are always still empty. Think of it differently: could the number in each cell mean something else? In the end, the answer has to appear on the start.
state-graph/level.order.mission.goal: Routes still only go right or down, but the robot walks backwards from the bottom-right corner. Build a board so that the start cell in the top-left corner ends up with the number of routes from start to end.
state-graph/level.order.mission.how: The This cell panel adds “is end”. If the robot reads a cell that is still empty, it stops.
state-graph/level.order.short: The machine turns round, so must the circuit
state-graph/level.order.tasks.order.diag: The robot walks from the bottom right to the top left, so when it reaches a cell, the cells above and to its left are still empty and can’t be read.
Counting from here to the end means counting back from the end. The 1 belongs on the end, not on the start.
state-graph/level.order.tasks.order.hint: On this machine, only right and down can be read. Leaving this cell, where can the first step go?
From the end to the end counts as 1 route: let a 1 through on “is end”.
The Route Counter works too: right into “up”, down into “left”, and is end into “start”.
state-graph/level.order.title: Work backwards
state-graph/level.pack.debrief.body.0: In puzzle 1, “priciest first” fell just short; in puzzle 2, “best value first” fell just short too. Greedy rules that look clever always have exceptions.
state-graph/level.pack.debrief.body.1: The safe way is to try every possible packing. 5 items give 32 packings, which is still manageable; 30 items give over a billion.
state-graph/level.pack.debrief.note: Greedy (always picking what looks best right now) doesn’t necessarily give the best result.
state-graph/level.pack.debrief.title: No easy shortcut
state-graph/level.pack.intro.0.t: A new chapter: packing a backpack. You are off on a trip, and the backpack has a weight limit. Each thing has a weight and a value, and you can take at most one of each. How do you pack to carry the most value?
state-graph/level.pack.intro.1.t: People often use one of two “shortcuts”: priciest first, or best value first (the highest value per kilogram). Go through the items in that order and pack each one that fits. Always grabbing what looks best right now is called being .
state-graph/level.pack.intro.2.t: This level has two puzzles. The side panel has two “Auto-pack” buttons, one for each shortcut. Try them first, then pack by hand to reach the target value.
state-graph/level.pack.mission.goal: The total weight can’t exceed the backpack’s limit, and you can take at most one of each item. Reach the target value in both puzzles.
state-graph/level.pack.mission.how: Click items to put them in or take them out. The two buttons in the side panel auto-pack using the shortcuts; give them a try.
state-graph/level.pack.title: Pack the backpack
state-graph/level.palin.debrief.body.0: Every cell of an interval table is computed from shorter stretches: with one end dropped, or both. So the short stretches have to come first: this machine goes by length from shortest to longest.
state-graph/level.palin.debrief.body.1: CHARACTER hides CARAC, and BBABCBCAB hides BABCBAB. Finding palindromic structures in DNA uses exactly this table.
state-graph/level.palin.debrief.note: Interval table: (i, j) holds the answer for a stretch, computed from shorter stretches.
state-graph/level.palin.debrief.title: The interval table
state-graph/level.palin.intro.0.t: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like ABA or RACECAR. If you delete some letters from a word (the rest keep their order), what is the longest palindrome you can leave? From CHARACTER, for example, you can leave CARAC.
state-graph/level.palin.intro.1.t: A new table: the interval table. Cell (i, j) holds the answer for “the stretch from letter i to letter j”. Only the upper-right half is used, because a stretch always starts to the left of where it ends. The top-right corner is the answer for the whole word.
state-graph/level.palin.intro.2.t: The diagonal holds single letters, each a palindrome of length 1 on its own, already filled in. The line just under the diagonal is “empty runs” with no letters at all, filled with 0.
state-graph/level.palin.intro.3.t: The robot stands on (i, j): the cell to the left is the stretch without its right end, the cell below is the stretch without its left end, and down-left is the stretch without both ends. The This cell panel has “ends match”. Look only at the two letters at the ends, and think what to do when they match and when they don’t.
state-graph/level.palin.intro.4.t: This robot scans by length: first every shortest stretch, then the longer ones, one diagonal at a time towards the top-right corner.
state-graph/level.palin.mission.goal: Find the longest palindromic subsequence in each word: the longest string, left after deleting some letters, that reads the same forwards and backwards.
state-graph/level.palin.mission.how: Build the circuit and click “Run tests”. The robot scans by length, so a long stretch only ever reads shorter stretches that are already computed.
state-graph/level.palin.tasks.palin.hint: When the ends match, both can stay. Which stretch is left, and how much do you add? Use a Pass gate with “ends match” as its condition.
When the ends differ, at least one has to go: drop the right end (left) or the left end (down), and take the larger. Wire all three into “max”.
No need to worry about the order: left, down and down-left are all shorter stretches, and since the robot scans by length they are always computed first.
state-graph/level.palin.title: Palindromes
state-graph/level.parity.debrief.body.0: “Exactly one is yes” is called XOR, and you built it from any-yes, Not and Pass gates alone.
state-graph/level.parity.debrief.body.1: A cell need not hold the whole number, only the part the question needs. Odd or even takes a single bit.
state-graph/level.parity.debrief.title: You built XOR
state-graph/level.parity.intro.0.t: Back to the grid city: only right or down. This time the question is not how many routes there are, but whether the number is odd or even. The table holds only yes / no: “yes” means odd.
state-graph/level.parity.intro.1.t: You only have the yes / no parts: any-yes, Not, the Pass gate and the Block gate.
state-graph/level.parity.mission.goal: Make every crossing hold “is the number of routes to here odd?”. The start counts as 1 route, which is odd.
state-graph/level.parity.short: Counting with only yes and no
state-graph/level.parity.tasks.parity.hi: Odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd: which mix of up and left makes a crossing odd?
Outside the city you get “—”, but here it should count as even (0 routes). An any-yes with a single input turns “—” into “no”.
state-graph/level.parity.title: Odd or even
state-graph/level.parse.debrief.body.0: 3 words, 2 ways; 4 words, 5; 5 words, 14: these are the Catalan numbers, and they grow very fast as words are added. That is why a computer analysing a sentence doesn’t list every tree, but works through this interval table cell by cell.
state-graph/level.parse.debrief.body.1: Real parsing (the CKY algorithm) also checks grammar rules: which two stretches can merge, and into what. The table has exactly the same shape.
state-graph/level.parse.debrief.note: Parse trees: “left × right” at each split point, then add them up.
state-graph/level.parse.debrief.title: Parsing
state-graph/level.parse.intro.0.t: “Old men and women”: are the women old too, or only the men? The same words, merged into phrases two at a time in different ways, mean different things: (old men) and women, or old (men and women). Draw the merging out and you get a parse tree.
state-graph/level.parse.intro.1.t: Suppose any two neighbouring stretches of words can be merged. How many different ways are there to merge a run of words? An interval table again: cell (i, j) records “how many ways words i to j can be merged”. A single word has just 1, so the diagonal is already filled in.
state-graph/level.parse.intro.2.t: The last merge joins a left stretch and a right stretch. At a given split point, the left side has some number of ways and the right side some number, and any left way can go with any right way: how many ways does this split point give? And how should the different split points be combined?
state-graph/level.parse.intro.3.t: When merging stones, each split point was “left + right”, and you picked the cheapest. What about here? Broom’s sweep arm sends the left parts and right parts by split point as before, and a Multiplier can multiply them pair by pair too.
state-graph/level.parse.mission.goal: A run of words is merged two at a time into phrases until it becomes one whole sentence. Work out how many different ways of merging there are (how many parse trees).
state-graph/level.parse.mission.how: The sweep arm sends the left part and right part for every split point.
state-graph/level.parse.short: How many ways can a sentence be read?
state-graph/level.parse.tasks.parse.hint: Look at a single split point first: every way on the left can go with every way on the right. How many is that in all?
Every split point’s result counts: wire them into “sum”.
state-graph/level.parse.title: The skeleton of a sentence
state-graph/level.pascal.debrief.body.0: Each brick’s number = right above + up-left. This is Pascal’s triangle, and also the number of ways to choose k things out of n.
state-graph/level.pascal.debrief.body.1: A table need not be square: any shape can be filled, as long as each cell knows its ways in.
state-graph/level.pascal.debrief.title: Pascal’s triangle
state-graph/level.pascal.intro.0.t: Bricks are stacked in a triangle: 1 brick in row 1, 2 in row 2, and so on. Starting from the top brick, each step goes to the brick right below or below-right.
state-graph/level.pascal.intro.1.t: The table becomes a triangle too: each row has only so many cells.
state-graph/level.pascal.mission.goal: How many ways are there down to the given brick of the last row?
state-graph/level.pascal.mission.how: Work one layer at a time, from left to right.
state-graph/level.pascal.tasks.pascal.di: Moving down only reaches the brick below or below-right, so the ways in are on the row above: right above and up-left.
state-graph/level.pascal.tasks.pascal.hi: Look only at the last step: before reaching this brick, which brick were you on?
Bricks on the triangle’s left and right edges can be reached from one brick only; the other side is “—”.
state-graph/level.pascal.title: Pascal’s triangle
state-graph/level.piles.debrief.body.0: Every “no” falls on a cell where A and B are both even. From such a position, whatever you take, your opponent can turn it back into “both piles even”.
state-graph/level.piles.debrief.body.1: This board has gone into your Parts as the <part-ref to="state-graph/judge"></part-ref>: it reads the three positions your opponent could face and decides whether this cell wins.
state-graph/level.piles.debrief.note: Two piles: each position = any (opponent’s position, negated).
state-graph/level.piles.debrief.title: A pattern on the board
state-graph/level.piles.intro.0.t: This time there are two piles of stones: pile A and pile B. On each move you can take 1 stone from one pile, or 1 from each pile. Whoever takes the last stone wins.
state-graph/level.piles.intro.1.t: This time “how many are left” takes two numbers, so the table becomes a board: row a, column b is the position “a left in pile A, b left in pile B”.
state-graph/level.piles.intro.2.t: The three moves land your opponent on the cells “one fewer in A” (up), “one fewer in B” (left) and “one fewer in each” (up-left). The rule is the same as in <level-ref to="state-graph/nim"></level-ref>. Once it is built, see what pattern grows across the whole board.
state-graph/level.piles.mission.goal: Each move takes 1 stone from one pile, or 1 from each; whoever takes the last stone wins. For every position, work out whether the player to move can win.
state-graph/level.piles.mission.how: This level checks the whole board. Once you pass, see how the “yes” and “no” cells are arranged.
state-graph/level.piles.short: A pattern of wins and losses
state-graph/level.piles.tasks.piles.hint: Three moves: “one fewer in A”, “one fewer in B” and “one fewer in each”. All three cells need reading.
Put a Not on each move, then wire them all into “any yes”.
state-graph/level.piles.title: Two piles
state-graph/level.pits.debrief.body.0: The Cheapest cell takes care of energy, the Block gate takes care of pits. Both are things you built or learned earlier; here you only wired them together.
state-graph/level.pits.debrief.body.1: A pit holds “—”, and “min” skips it, so routes through a pit drop out by themselves.
state-graph/level.pits.debrief.title: Parts on parts
state-graph/level.pits.intro.0.t: In this city every crossing costs energy, and some have caved in and can’t be passed at all.
state-graph/level.pits.mission.goal: Only right or down, avoiding every pit. Going from the top left to the bottom right, what is the least energy you can spend?
state-graph/level.pits.tasks.pits.diagno: Some crossings are pits and can’t be passed. Read “is rock”.
Energy and pits: have you handled each of them before?
Cut off the pits: a Block gate outputs “—” when its condition is “yes”.
state-graph/level.pits.title: Pits and prices
state-graph/level.prefix.debrief.body.0: Both ways give the same answers. But the sweep arm reads n cells at house n, so 100 houses take 5,050 reads in all; using the cell on the left, each house reads just 1 cell, 100 in all.
state-graph/level.prefix.debrief.body.1: If the previous cell has already stored the answer, don’t sweep again from the start: that is an old rule of dynamic programming.
state-graph/level.prefix.debrief.note: Prefix sums: total up to this house = total up to the previous one + this house. If the last cell will do, don’t sweep again.
state-graph/level.prefix.debrief.title: If the last cell will do, don’t sweep again
state-graph/level.prefix.intro.0.t: A new chapter and a new robot: Broom. It has a <part-ref to="state-graph/sweep"></part-ref> that sweeps a whole run of cells in one go and feeds every number in the run into the circuit board.
state-graph/level.prefix.intro.1.t: Along a street, each house has some money at its door. Under each house the robot must write: how much money there is in total from house 1 up to this one.
state-graph/level.prefix.intro.2.t: What the sweep arm sends is a whole run: its wire on the circuit board is drawn thicker. A Merger can take a whole run directly, and every number in it takes part.
state-graph/level.prefix.mission.goal: Under each house, write how much money there is in total from house 1 up to this one.
state-graph/level.prefix.mission.how: This level has two tasks and checks the whole row. Use the sweep arm first; once you pass, the arm is folded away.
state-graph/level.prefix.short: A sweep arm reads a whole run at once
The sweep arm is folded away: use only the cell on the left and this house’s money.
Total up to this house = total up to the previous house + this house’s money.
Read “previous” and “this house’s money”, and wire them into an Adder.
state-graph/level.prefix.tasks.prefix.as: Use the sweep arm to bring in the money from house 1 to this one in one go, and add it up.
state-graph/level.prefix.tasks.prefix.do: But at every house, the sweep arm sweeps again from house 1: house 100 means reading 100 cells.
Doesn’t the cell on the left already hold “the total up to the previous house”? In the next task, the sweep arm is folded away.
state-graph/level.prefix.tasks.prefix.hi: Click the <part-ref to="state-graph/sweep"></part-ref> under the view to read the whole run it passes over.
Wire the whole run into a “sum” Merger, then wire that to this cell.
state-graph/level.prefix.title: Everything before
state-graph/level.reach.debrief.body.0: Cells don’t have to hold numbers. Store “yes / no” and the table can answer “can it be done?” questions.
state-graph/level.reach.debrief.body.1: The way of merging changes with it: counting routes means adding up, but for “can you get there” a single “yes” is enough, so you use “any yes”. In test 2, a line of rocks blocks the way completely, and the end is “no”.
state-graph/level.reach.debrief.note: Cells can hold “yes / no”: if any way in can be reached, so can this cell.
state-graph/level.reach.debrief.title: Yes or no fills a table too
state-graph/level.reach.intro.0.t: Sometimes you don’t need to know how many routes there are, only whether you can get there at all. Then the cells don’t need to hold numbers: “yes” or “no” is enough.
state-graph/level.reach.intro.1.t: A new component: the “any yes” Merger. If any signal wired into it is “yes”, it outputs “yes”. At a crossing, if either up or left can be reached, so can this one.
state-graph/level.reach.intro.2.t: The start can of course be reached. What about rock cells? The Block gate can now block “yes / no” too: a blocked cell gets “—”, and “any yes” won’t count it as a “yes”.
state-graph/level.reach.mission.goal: Only right or down, and never through a rock. Write “yes” or “no” in every cell: can you get here from the start? (Rock cells get “—”.)
state-graph/level.reach.mission.how: This level checks the whole table. Read up, left and “is start”, merge them with an “any yes” Merger, and don’t forget the rocks.
state-graph/level.reach.tasks.reach.hint: This cell can be reached if either up or left can: wire both up and left into an “any yes” Merger.
The start can be reached: wire “is start” into “any yes” too.
Nobody can reach a rock cell: block the result with a Block gate, its condition wired to “is rock”.
state-graph/level.reach.title: Can you get there
state-graph/level.replace.debrief.body.0: Up-left only: everything before is fixed, and this letter either stays or is swapped.
state-graph/level.replace.debrief.title: Down the diagonal
state-graph/level.replace.intro.0.t: Spelling correction: when a word is mistyped, see how far it is from the right one. In this level only one kind of change is allowed: swap one letter for another, 1 step each. The two words are the same length.
state-graph/level.replace.intro.1.t: The table is still the alignment table: one word along the top, one down the left. With swaps only, letter i on the left only ever lines up with letter i on top, so the answer comes down the diagonal.
state-graph/level.replace.mission.goal: Work out the fewest letters to swap to turn the word on the left into the word on top.
state-graph/level.replace.mission.how: The cell up-left means “all the letters before are already fixed”.
This level only allows swaps, so up and left are no use: look only at up-left.
If the letters match, nothing to swap: keep up-left as it is. If they differ, swap one: up-left + 1. Take the smaller.
The start is two empty words: 0 steps.
state-graph/level.replace.title: Change a letter
state-graph/level.ring.debrief.body.0: A ring won’t straighten out, so split it into cases: on layer A the first house is left alone and the rest is a straight street; on layer B the last is. Take the better of the two layers.
state-graph/level.ring.debrief.body.1: Splitting into cases is remembering one more thing too: which case you are in.
state-graph/level.ring.debrief.title: Split into two cases
state-graph/level.ring.intro.0.t: This street runs round in a ring: the first and the last house are neighbours too, and can’t both be robbed.
state-graph/level.ring.intro.1.t: The table has two layers, A and B, each the two rows of <level-ref to="state-graph/robber"></level-ref>: this house skipped, this house robbed. What each layer records is up to you; the cell’s facts include “is the first house”, “is the last house” and “is layer A”.
state-graph/level.ring.mission.goal: No two neighbouring houses, and the first and the last count as neighbours. Work out the most money you can steal.
state-graph/level.ring.mission.how: The answer is the largest cell in the last column of either layer.
The ends can’t both be robbed, so every plan leaves at least one of them alone. Could each layer take one of those cases?
On which layer is “robbed” stopped, and at which house? “Is layer A” can be a gate’s condition.
state-graph/level.ring.title: A ring of houses
state-graph/level.rising.debrief.body.0: This cell’s ways in are no longer one or two fixed cells, but every earlier cell that meets the condition, and how many there are depends on the data.
state-graph/level.rising.debrief.body.1: This problem is called the <wiki-ref to="state-graph/lis"></wiki-ref>: the most days you can pick from a run of share prices with each day higher than the last, or the longest upgrade path through a pile of versions, both come down to it.
state-graph/level.rising.debrief.note: The way in can be a whole run: take the max over the cells of every shorter post, then + 1.
state-graph/level.rising.debrief.title: Longest increasing subsequence
state-graph/level.rising.intro.0.t: A row of posts of different heights. Pick some from left to right so that each is taller than the one before; you may skip posts in between. What is the most you can pick?
state-graph/level.rising.intro.1.t: Each cell records: ending with this post, the longest run you can make. The answer for the whole row is the largest cell in the row.
state-graph/level.rising.intro.2.t: Look only at the last post: which post comes before it? It can be any earlier post, as long as it is shorter. However many posts come before, that is how many ways in there may be. That is exactly the sweep arm’s job: it brings in every earlier cell (the answer recorded under each post) at once.
state-graph/level.rising.intro.3.t: Treat the “S” cell on the far left as a post shorter than all the others, holding 0: coming after it means this post is the first. This machine’s sweep arm has a filter: it keeps only the posts shorter than this one, and the cells it drops are dimmed in the view.
state-graph/level.rising.mission.goal: Pick posts from left to right, each taller than the last (skipping is allowed). For each post, work out the longest run that ends with it; the answer for the row is the largest of these.
state-graph/level.rising.mission.how: This level checks the whole row. The sweep arm only brings in posts shorter than this one; the cells it filters out are dimmed.
state-graph/level.rising.tasks.rising.hi: This post can follow any post shorter than it: click the sweep arm, and it brings in only the posts shorter than this one.
Pick the largest of the cells that remain, then count this post itself: max, then + 1.
state-graph/level.rising.title: Ever taller
state-graph/level.robber.debrief.body.0: With one cell per house, that cell has to stand for both “this house was robbed” and “this house was skipped”, but their futures differ: the first can’t rob the next house, the second can.
state-graph/level.robber.debrief.body.1: With an extra layer, each case gets a cell of its own, and the machine no longer mixes them up.
state-graph/level.robber.debrief.body.2: A good state remembers everything that can affect the future. This is the hardest, and the most important, step in designing a dynamic program.
state-graph/level.robber.debrief.note: A state must remember everything that affects the future. If it falls short, add a layer.
state-graph/level.robber.debrief.title: Remember one more thing, and it’s solved
state-graph/level.robber.intro.0.t: A new chapter and a new puzzle. A street has a row of houses, each with some money hidden inside. A thief can’t rob two neighboring houses, or the alarm goes off. What is the most money the thief can take?
state-graph/level.robber.intro.1.t: For example, robbing #1, #3 and #5 gives 2 + 9 + 1 = 12. Robbing #2 and #4 gives only 7 + 3 = 10.
state-graph/level.robber.intro.2.t: This chapter’s robot is Layercake: its view is only 3×3, so at each house it sees only the previous house’s cell, nothing earlier. In the view, the red frame is this house and the cell to its left is the previous one; in the This cell panel, “this house’s money” is the money hidden in this house.
state-graph/level.robber.intro.3.t: To get the most money, merging should take the larger value, so the components now include a “max” Merger. First try with a single row of cells, each recording “the most that can be stolen from the first i houses”. If it fails, read the reason carefully: it will tell you something very important.
state-graph/level.robber.mission.goal: Robbing two neighboring houses sets off the alarm. Work out the most money that can be stolen on each street.
state-graph/level.robber.mission.how: Build a board and give it a try. The first failure in this level is part of the plan, so read the reason carefully.
state-graph/level.robber.short: One number can’t remember it all
If this house is skipped, the previous one may or may not have been robbed: skipped = max(prev skipped, prev robbed).
This house can only be robbed if the previous one was skipped: robbed = prev skipped + this house’s money.
After this house, it may or may not have been robbed: most so far = max(skipped, robbed).

Each house now has three cells, and the robot stands on the middle one. In the view, the column of red frames is, from top to bottom, “skipped”, “robbed” and “most so far”; the column to the left is the previous house’s three cells. House 0 is before anything starts: skipped = 0, robbed = — (impossible).
Unlocked <part-ref to="state-graph/layer"></part-ref>: each house now has three cells
state-graph/level.robber.tasks.robber.on: On street {test} the most that can be stolen is {want}, but the machine computed {got}. This time the problem isn’t your circuit: as long as each house has only one cell, any wiring will go wrong. Look at this counterexample:
One number can’t remember it all
Add a layer to the state
state-graph/level.robber.title: No two in a row
state-graph/level.rocks.debrief.body.0: Once a rock cell outputs “—”, every route through it is cut off: Mergers skip “—”, so it adds nothing to the cells after it.
state-graph/level.rocks.debrief.body.1: Nothing inside the Route Counter had to change. You just added a gate outside it. A finished part can be used as it is, with a little something new added to handle a new situation.
state-graph/level.rocks.debrief.note: A cell that can’t be passed outputs “—”, which rules out every route through it.
state-graph/level.rocks.debrief.title: The rocks cut the routes
state-graph/level.rocks.intro.0.t: In a mountain city, some crossings are blocked by fallen rocks (the hatched cells), and no route may pass through them.
state-graph/level.rocks.intro.1.t: The tray holds the <part-ref to="state-graph/counter"></part-ref>: it adds up its “up” and “left” ports, plus 1 when its “start” port is “yes”.
state-graph/level.rocks.intro.2.t: This level’s This cell panel adds “is rock”, and the tray has a new component: the Block gate. It is the exact opposite of the Pass gate: when its condition is “yes” it outputs “—”; otherwise it lets the number through unchanged.
state-graph/level.rocks.intro.3.t: Think about it: how many routes from the start to a rock cell can actually be traveled? What should a rock cell output?
state-graph/level.rocks.mission.goal: Only right or down, and no route may pass through a rock cell (hatched). Have the robot count the routes correctly in cities with rockfalls too.
state-graph/level.rocks.mission.how: The Route Counter is in the tray, ready to go on the board.
state-graph/level.rocks.short: Add a gate outside the part
state-graph/level.rocks.tasks.rocks.hint: Routes can’t pass through rocks. How many routes from the start can actually get to a rock cell?
Place a Route Counter and a Block gate: wire This cell’s “is rock” to the gate’s condition port and the Route Counter into its number port, then wire the Block gate to “this cell”.
state-graph/level.rocks.title: Rockfall
state-graph/level.roll.debrief.body.0: Rewriting from right to left, dp[w − weight] hasn’t been touched by this item yet, so it reads an old value: each item at most once.
state-graph/level.roll.debrief.body.1: Rewriting from left to right, dp[w − weight] may already include this item, and taking it again is just right: each item as many times as you like.
state-graph/level.roll.debrief.body.2: The same circuit board, just a different direction, solves two different problems. Keeping only one row like this is called a rolling array, and it can squash a table thousands of rows tall into a single row.
state-graph/level.roll.debrief.note: One row rewritten in place: right to left, once each; left to right, unlimited.
state-graph/level.roll.debrief.title: Direction is meaning
state-graph/level.roll.intro.0.t: Look closely at the knapsack table: each row only uses the row above. So why keep the whole table? Keep just one row, and rewrite it in place for each item.
state-graph/level.roll.intro.1.t: Rewriting in place carries a risk: rewriting dp[w] reads dp[w − weight]. If that cell has already been rewritten this round, what you read is a value where the item “has already been taken”.
state-graph/level.roll.intro.2.t: This level has two kinds of backpack: one where each item can be taken at most once, and one where each item can be taken many times (like a shop with plenty of everything). The board isn’t hard: new dp[w] = max(old dp[w], dp[w − weight] + value). The red frame dp[w] in the view is where the new value is written, and clicking it in the view reads the old value before it is rewritten; dp[w − weight] is what the telescopic arm reaches.
state-graph/level.roll.intro.3.t: The real trick is the machine’s : when each item can be taken at most once, it rewrites right to left; when each item can be taken many times, it rewrites left to right. Why does the same circuit board give different answers when only the direction changes?
state-graph/level.roll.mission.goal: In one kind of backpack each item can be taken at most once; in the other, many times. Either way, the total weight can’t exceed the capacity. Build the circuit so that all four tests come out right.
state-graph/level.roll.mission.how: Yellow is the cell being rewritten; red means a value rewritten earlier this round was read.
state-graph/level.roll.short: The rewrite direction is the meaning
state-graph/level.roll.tasks.roll.diagno: The circuit board: new dp[w] = max(old dp[w], dp[w − weight] + value). All three need reading in: the old dp[w], dp[w − weight] and the item value.
state-graph/level.roll.title: Squash it into one row
<level-ref to="state-graph/cheapest"></level-ref> added and took the min; here you multiply and take the max. The operations changed; the skeleton did not.
state-graph/level.safefrog.debrief.title: Multiply, then take the max
state-graph/level.safefrog.intro.0.t: Some stones are steady and some are slippery. Under each stone is the chance the frog keeps its footing, 0.9 meaning nine times out of ten. A route needs every stone to hold, so the chances multiply: 0.9 × 0.5 = 0.45.
state-graph/level.safefrog.intro.1.t: A new part, the <part-ref to="part:table/mul"></part-ref>: it outputs a × b.
state-graph/level.safefrog.mission.goal: Find the steadiest way across: what is the best chance the frog has of reaching the last stone safely?
state-graph/level.safefrog.mission.how: Jumps work as <level-ref to="state-graph/frogfar"></level-ref>: from the stone before, or from the ↶ stone. The bank is solid: its chance is 1.
state-graph/level.safefrog.tasks.safefro: The steadiest route to this stone = the steadiest route to where it came from × this stone’s chance of holding.
Of the two places it can come from, pick the steadier: take the max.
state-graph/level.safefrog.title: A safe crossing
state-graph/level.seam.debrief.body.0: Each cell = its own energy + the smallest of the three cells above. Just like <level-ref to="state-graph/cheapest"></level-ref>, only with the ways in turned round.
state-graph/level.seam.debrief.body.1: The seam runs through the background and skirts the letters’ edges: their energy is too high, so crossing them is too “expensive”.
state-graph/level.seam.debrief.note: Seam: each cell = its own energy + the smallest of up-left, up and up-right.
state-graph/level.seam.debrief.title: A seam is a cheapest route too
state-graph/level.seam.intro.0.t: Now for real pictures. A picture is a table too, with one pixel per cell. This chapter’s pictures come from Vision Complete’s test images: a few bright letters on a grey background.
state-graph/level.seam.intro.1.t: You want to make the picture a little narrower without squashing the letters. The trick is to find a seam from the top row to the bottom row: one pixel per row, each step going straight down, down-left or down-right. Take that seam out and the picture is one column narrower.
state-graph/level.seam.intro.2.t: Which seam is least noticeable to remove? Look at the energy: the more a pixel differs from its neighbours left and right, above and below, the higher its energy (the edges of letters), while flat background has very little. The edges you computed in Vision Complete are the energy here. The lower a seam’s total energy, the better.
state-graph/level.seam.intro.3.t: Isn’t this just ? Only now you walk from top to bottom, and the ways in are the three cells up-left, up and up-right. Each cell of the table records “the least energy a seam from the top row to here can cost”; the smallest cell in the bottom row is the energy of the whole seam. The small number in a cell’s corner is that pixel’s own energy.
state-graph/level.seam.mission.goal: Find the lowest-energy seam in each picture: from the top row to the bottom row, one pixel per row, each step going straight down, down-left or down-right; a seam’s energy is the sum of the pixel energies along it.
state-graph/level.seam.mission.how: This level checks the whole table. Once you pass, the seam is marked on the small picture to the left.
state-graph/level.seam.short: The cheapest route through a picture
state-graph/level.seam.tasks.seam.diagno: Looking only straight up, a seam can only be a dead-straight vertical line, and cutting it out would slice through the middle of a letter. At each step a seam may slant one cell down-left or down-right, so up-left and up-right are ways in too.
Three ways in: up-left, up and up-right. Take the min.
Then add this pixel’s own energy. There is nothing above the top row: use a Pass gate to let a 0 in on the top row (just like the start in <level-ref to="state-graph/cheapest"></level-ref>).
state-graph/level.seam.title: The least noticeable seam
A single column has only one seam, and the table just adds the energy down cell by cell.
state-graph/level.seamline.debrief.title: Added all the way down
state-graph/level.seamline.intro.0.t: A picture just 1 pixel wide. Every pixel has an energy, written in its cell’s top-left corner: the more it stands out, the higher its energy.
state-graph/level.seamline.intro.1.t: A seam runs from the top to the bottom, through one pixel in each row. A seam’s energy is the total energy of the pixels it passes through.
state-graph/level.seamline.mission.goal: What is the total energy of the seam from top to bottom? Each cell holds “the energy from the top down to here”.
state-graph/level.seamline.mission.how: Row by row, from the top down.
state-graph/level.seamline.short: Energy, added all the way down
state-graph/level.seamline.tasks.seamlin: The energy down to this cell = the energy down to the cell above + this cell’s own.
Above the top row there is nothing: feed a 0 in on the top row.
state-graph/level.seamline.title: A single column
state-graph/level.seamslant.debrief.body: The same skeleton as <level-ref to="state-graph/cheapest"></level-ref>: take the min, then add this cell. Only the ways in grew from two to three on the row above, and the start from one cell to the whole top row.
state-graph/level.seamslant.intro.0.t: Now the picture has several columns. A seam starts at any pixel of the top row, and each step goes to the pixel right below, below-left or below-right, all the way to the bottom row.
state-graph/level.seamslant.mission.goal: What is the energy of the lowest-energy seam? The answer is the smallest number in the bottom row.
state-graph/level.seamslant.mission.how: Row by row, from the top down.
state-graph/level.seamslant.short: Start anywhere on the top row
state-graph/level.seamslant.tasks.seamsl: Each step of a seam may go below-left, straight down or below-right: up-left, up and up-right on the row above are all ways in.
Before reaching this cell, which pixels of the row above could the seam be on?
Pick the lowest of them, then add this cell’s own energy.
state-graph/level.seamslant.title: It may slant
state-graph/level.segment.debrief.body.0: Chinese has no spaces, so input methods and search engines segment words first, with this very board: try every cut, add the part’s cost, keep the cheapest.
state-graph/level.segment.debrief.body.1: “The fewest parts” and <level-ref to="state-graph/wordcost"></level-ref> are its special cases: every cost 1, or no single letters to fall back on.
state-graph/level.segment.debrief.title: Word segmentation
state-graph/level.segment.intro.0.t: A real sentence: not every word is in the dictionary, and names and new words often aren’t. Whatever can’t be found is cut one letter to a part, at a high price per letter.
state-graph/level.segment.intro.1.t: That way every sentence can be cut, and known words are always cheaper.
state-graph/level.segment.mission.goal: Work out what the cheapest cut of each sentence costs.
state-graph/level.segment.mission.how: What a single letter costs is shown at the end of the dictionary.
A single letter is just another part, with its cost in the dictionary.
state-graph/level.segment.title: Word segmentation
state-graph/level.slant.debrief.body.0: The Route Counter’s ports say “up” and “left”, yet you wired in “left” and “up-left”, and it still got the right answer.
state-graph/level.slant.debrief.body.1: A part cares about structure, not names: add two sources, with 1 at the start. Whenever a new problem has this structure, the old part can be used as it is.
state-graph/level.slant.debrief.note: A part cares only about structure: two sources added, 1 at the start. It works in any direction.
state-graph/level.slant.debrief.title: Parts don’t care about direction
state-graph/level.slant.intro.0.t: Back to the slanted streets: each step goes one cell right, or one cell diagonally down and right. No energy this time: starting from the top-left corner, how many routes reach the bottom-right corner?
state-graph/level.slant.intro.1.t: Look only at the last step: you reach this crossing either from the left, or diagonally from the up-left. You can’t get here from above.
state-graph/level.slant.intro.2.t: The Route Counter’s three ports are labeled “up”, “left” and “start”, but all it really does is add up the first two, with 1 at the start. Whichever two cells you wire into it, those are the two it adds.
state-graph/level.slant.mission.goal: Each step goes one cell right, or one cell diagonally down and right. Work out how many routes lead from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.
state-graph/level.slant.mission.how: Click the cells and facts this level needs, then place components and wire them. Cells that can’t be reached will be “—”.
state-graph/level.slant.tasks.slant.diag: In this city you can’t go straight down, so nothing arrives from above.
state-graph/level.slant.tasks.slant.hint: The last step into a crossing comes either from the left (one cell right) or from the up-left (one cell diagonally).
Wire “left” into the Route Counter’s “up” port, “up-left” into its “left” port, and “is start” into its “start” port. The port names don’t matter; it just adds two numbers.
state-graph/level.slant.title: Slanted streets
state-graph/level.slantcost.debrief.body: A crossing out of reach has no way in, so the min gives “—”. The “sum” Merger skips that “—” and keeps just the energy, so the crossing suddenly holds a number, and later crossings may pick it.
The Adder outputs “—” whenever either side is “—”: a crossing out of reach stays “—”, and later crossings skip it when they take the min.
state-graph/level.slantcost.debrief.note: Adder: if either side is “—”, so is the result. The “sum” Merger skips “—”.
state-graph/level.slantcost.debrief.titl: Out of reach stays out of reach
state-graph/level.slantcost.intro.0.t: In another city the streets are slanted: each step goes one cell right, or one cell diagonally down and right. Every crossing still costs energy. Going from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner, what is the least energy you can spend?
state-graph/level.slantcost.intro.1.t: The last step into a crossing comes either from the left or diagonally from the up-left. In this city, some crossings can’t be reached from the start at all.
state-graph/level.slantcost.intro.2.t: This level’s board becomes the part , to be used where more ways lead in, so the board has one more input, “way in 3”. This city has no third way in, so it is always “—”; wire it into the min together with left and up-left, and the part gets three ways in.
state-graph/level.slantcost.intro.3.t: A new component: the <part-ref to="part:table/add"></part-ref>, which outputs a + b. It differs from the “sum” Merger: if either side is “—”, the result is “—”.
state-graph/level.slantcost.mission.goal: Each step goes one cell right or one cell diagonally down and right, and every crossing you pass through (start and end included) costs the energy in its top-left corner. Work out the least energy needed to get from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.
state-graph/level.slantcost.mission.how: In the view, “up-left” is the cell a diagonal step comes from. If a test fails, look at what the robot wrote on the crossings it can’t reach.
state-graph/level.slantcost.tasks.slantc: In this city you can’t go straight down, so nothing arrives from above.
Leaving the top left and going only right or down-right, can you ever reach the bottom-left corner? What should be written there?
The “sum” Merger skips “—”, so a crossing out of reach still turns into a number once its energy is added. Add the energy with an Adder.
At the start every way in is “—”, so the Adder gives “—” too. Use a Pass gate to send a 0 into the min at the start (once the Constant is on the board, click it to change it to 0).
“Way in 3” is always “—” in this level, but it is one of the part’s ports too: wire it into the min together with left and up-left.
state-graph/level.slantcost.title: Out of reach
state-graph/level.slip.debrief.body.0: Because the robot can slip, every cell along the cliff edge gets “worse”: it may be one step from the treasure, but going right carries a 20% chance of falling off. Look at the arrows: hugging the cliff, the robot prefers the direction where a slip does no harm.
state-graph/level.slip.debrief.body.1: Weighting each outcome by how likely it is gives the . Making decisions step by step under uncertainty is called a Markov decision process, the mathematical skeleton of reinforcement learning.
state-graph/level.slip.debrief.note: When the outcome is uncertain, an action’s value = each outcome weighted by how likely it is.
state-graph/level.slip.debrief.title: Expectation
state-graph/level.slip.intro.0.t: Ice is slippery. In this level the robot moves only right or down, but every step has a 20% chance of sliding the other way: aiming right, it may slide down; aiming down, it may slide right.
state-graph/level.slip.intro.1.t: The bottom row and right-hand column of the map are cliffs (−10), and the treasure sits right at the cliff edge.
state-graph/level.slip.intro.2.t: When the outcome is uncertain, an action’s value is its outcomes weighted by how likely they are: going right = 0.8 × right + 0.2 × down. Pick the better of the two actions, then discount by 10%.
state-graph/level.slip.intro.3.t: The circuit will be fairly big. A tip: one Constant can be wired into several Multipliers at once.
state-graph/level.slip.mission.goal: Move only right or down; every step has a 20% chance of sliding the other way. Each cell’s value = 0.9 × the better of the two actions; going right = 0.8 × right + 0.2 × down, going down = 0.8 × down + 0.2 × right.
state-graph/level.slip.mission.how: This level checks the whole table. Once you pass, each cell grows an arrow for its best action.
The “go right” action: 0.8 × right + 0.2 × down. Two Multipliers and an Adder.
Take the larger of the two actions, then multiply by 0.9.
state-graph/level.slip.title: A slippery floor
state-graph/level.spell.debrief.body.0: This is how keyboards and search boxes come up with “Did you mean…?”: compare the typed word with each candidate in the dictionary and pick the one with the smallest edit distance.
state-graph/level.spell.debrief.body.1: You didn’t build a new circuit: you just took the Edit Distance part and wired it into a new problem.
state-graph/level.spell.debrief.note: Spelling correction: work out the edit distance to each candidate and pick the smallest.
state-graph/level.spell.debrief.title: Correction
state-graph/level.spell.intro.0.t: You typed ACROS. The dictionary has a few candidate words: which one is closest to it?
state-graph/level.spell.intro.1.t: “Closest” means fewest changes: the <wiki-ref to="state-graph/edit"></wiki-ref>. The <part-ref to="state-graph/cost"></part-ref> in the tray works it out.
state-graph/level.spell.intro.2.t: Each test is one candidate word. Once all three tests pass, see which candidate needs the fewest steps.
state-graph/level.spell.mission.goal: Work out the edit distance between the typo ACROS and each candidate word (delete, insert and replace each count as 1 step).
state-graph/level.spell.mission.how: The <part-ref to="state-graph/cost"></part-ref> is in the tray: just wire up its five inputs.
state-graph/level.spell.short: Edit distance, put to work on typos
state-graph/level.spell.tasks.spell.hint: The Edit Distance Meter’s five inputs: up-left, up, left, letters match, is start. Wire them up to match.
state-graph/level.spell.title: Did you mean…?
state-graph/level.stairs.debrief.body.0: If you used the Route Counter, you’ll have noticed: it has no idea it is counting stairs, and yet it got them right.
state-graph/level.stairs.debrief.body.1: City crossings and staircases look completely unrelated, but they share a structure: every cell’s answer comes from a few earlier cells, plus a starting point. Learning to see that structure is the most important step in learning dynamic programming.
state-graph/level.stairs.debrief.note: Climbing stairs: step i = step i − 1 + step i − 2, with the ground counting as 1 way.
state-graph/level.stairs.debrief.title: 5, 13 and 55 ways
state-graph/level.stairs.intro.0.t: A different problem. When you climb stairs, each stride can go up 1 step or 2 steps. How many different ways are there to reach step n?
state-graph/level.stairs.intro.1.t: Treat each step as a cell and lay them out in a row. Step 0 is the ground.
state-graph/level.stairs.intro.2.t: The last stride onto step 5 is either 1 step up from step 4, or 2 steps up from step 3.
state-graph/level.stairs.intro.3.t: This time the robot walks along the row of steps, starting from the ground (step 0) and moving right one step at a time. But the step 2 below is two cells away, out of reach of a 3×3 view. So for this level your robot is upgraded to Farsight, with a 5×5 view. In the This cell panel, “is ground” is “yes” only on step 0.
state-graph/level.stairs.intro.4.t: Build a board. With Boxy you found that parts care about structure, not names. Have you seen the structure of stair climbing somewhere before?
state-graph/level.stairs.mission.goal: Each stride goes up 1 or 2 steps, starting from the ground (step 0). Work out how many ways there are to reach steps 4, 6 and 9.
state-graph/level.stairs.mission.how: The robot goes up from step 0 (the ground), one step at a time. Standing on the ground counts as 1 way. In the view, one cell left of the red frame is 1 step down, and two cells left is 2 steps down.
state-graph/level.stairs.short: A different view, the same structure
state-graph/level.stairs.tasks.stairs.hi: The last stride might be 1 step or 2 steps: add up “1 step down” and “2 steps down”.
The ground counts as 1 way: wire “is ground” into a Pass gate’s condition port and a Constant 1 into its number port.
You can also use the Route Counter directly: 1 step down into its “up”, 2 steps down into “left”, and is ground into “start”.
state-graph/level.stairs.title: Climbing stairs
state-graph/level.stamp.debrief.body.0: A Pass gate is like a door: on the start it opens and a 1 goes into the Merger; on any other cell it stays shut, and the Merger adds only up and left.
state-graph/level.stamp.debrief.body.1: It got all three cities right: 3×4, 4×4 and 5×6. Give it a 100×100 city and the same board works just as well.
state-graph/level.stamp.debrief.body.2: Every cell’s answer is computed from the answers of earlier cells and then recorded in the table. This method has a proper name: dynamic programming.
state-graph/level.stamp.debrief.note: Wire the rule into a circuit and the machine can fill a table of any size. That is dynamic programming.
state-graph/level.stamp.debrief.title: Your first machine
state-graph/level.stamp.intro.0.t: In this level the start is no longer filled in. The board holds the circuit you wired in <level-ref to="state-graph/confluence"></level-ref>. When the robot reaches the start, up and left are both “out”, so the Merger receives nothing and can only output “—”, and every crossing after it reads nothing but “—”.
state-graph/level.stamp.intro.1.t: Under the view there is a This cell panel. Its “is start” is “yes” only while the robot stands on the start, and “no” on every other cell. Click it, and the This cell part on the left of the circuit board gains an output sending a yes / no signal: a diamond dot and a dashed wire.
state-graph/level.stamp.intro.2.t: Two new components: a <part-ref to="part:table/const"></part-ref> always outputs the same number; a <part-ref to="part:table/pass"></part-ref> lets its number through only when its condition port receives “yes”, and otherwise outputs “—”.
state-graph/level.stamp.mission.goal: Only right or down, and the start is no longer filled in. Have the robot write 1 on the start and up + left on every other crossing, so it counts the routes correctly in all three cities.
state-graph/level.stamp.mission.how: Click “is start” in the inputs window: the This cell part gets an output for it. If a test fails, the robot stops on the cell where it went wrong, and the numbers in the view and on the board are what it saw and computed there.
state-graph/level.stamp.tasks.stamp.diag: The robot walks from the top left to the bottom right, so when it reaches a cell, the cells to its right and below are still empty and can’t be read.
With the Constant wired straight into the Merger, every crossing gets an extra 1. Use a Pass gate so it only goes through at the start.
state-graph/level.stamp.tasks.stamp.guid: Step 1: click “is start” under This cell.
Step 2: drag a <part-ref to="part:table/const"></part-ref> and a <part-ref to="part:table/pass"></part-ref> from the tray onto the board.
state-graph/level.stamp.tasks.stamp.hint: What should the start hold? That number must appear only on the start, while every other crossing stays up + left.
Wire “is start” into a Pass gate’s “if” port and a Constant 1 into its “num” port, then wire the Pass gate into the Merger’s free dot.
state-graph/level.stamp.title: Spot the start
state-graph/level.stock1.debrief.body.0: Each layer holds “the most money you can have today, ending today in this state”. Buying and selling just move you from one layer to another.
state-graph/level.stock1.debrief.title: The state became layers
state-graph/level.stock1.intro.0.t: You know a stock’s price on each of the coming days. You may buy once and sell once, buying first. How much can you make at most?
state-graph/level.stock1.intro.1.t: At the end of each day you are in one of three states: not bought yet, holding, or sold. Each state is a layer, with a column for each day.
state-graph/level.stock1.intro.2.t: Every layer runs the same board. The cell to the left is the same layer the day before; the probe reads the layer you come from, the day before. What stepping over from there brings in is in the This cell panel: buying pays today’s price, selling earns it.
state-graph/level.stock1.mission.goal: Work out the most money you can make. Not trading at all is allowed, which makes 0.
state-graph/level.stock1.mission.how: The answer is the larger of the “not bought yet” and “sold” layers on the last day.
state-graph/level.stock1.short: Which layer you are on each day
state-graph/level.stock1.tasks.stock1.di: Buying and selling both change layer: the probe reads the layer you come from, the day before.
state-graph/level.stock1.tasks.stock1.hi: Stay as you were, or step over from where you come from? Take the larger.
Stepping over = what the probe reads + what the step brings in.
state-graph/level.stock1.title: Buy once, sell once
state-graph/level.stones.debrief.body.0: Each cell’s ways in are all its split points: the longer the run, the more split points. This “the last step joins two parts” structure is called interval dynamic programming.
state-graph/level.stones.debrief.body.1: Bracketing a chain of calculations, the best order for multiplying a chain of matrices, merging a row of neighbouring files two at a time: all of these use this kind of interval table. This board has gone into your Parts as the <part-ref to="state-graph/interval"></part-ref>.
state-graph/level.stones.debrief.note: Interval merging: the last step joins a left part and a right part; pick the cheapest split point, then add the cost of the whole run.
state-graph/level.stones.debrief.title: Interval merging
state-graph/level.stones.intro.0.t: A row of stone piles. Each move merges two neighbouring piles into one, at a cost equal to their combined weight. Keep going until only one pile is left. What is the least it can cost?
state-graph/level.stones.intro.1.t: Take 3, 1, 2: merge 3 and 1 first (cost 4), then with 2 (cost 6), 10 in all; or merge 1 and 2 first (cost 3), then with 3 (cost 6), 9 in all. A different order, a different cost.
state-graph/level.stones.intro.2.t: An interval table again: cell (i, j) records “the least it costs to merge piles i to j into one”. A single pile needs no merging, so the diagonal is already filled with 0.
state-graph/level.stones.intro.3.t: The last merge always joins one big pile on the left with one big pile on the right. Where do left and right divide? It could be any split point. Think: what does this last merge cost? And which two cells of the table hold the cost of everything before it?
state-graph/level.stones.intro.4.t: This time Broom’s sweep arm works by split point: each split point sends a pair of cells, lined up as two whole runs, “left parts” and “right parts”. An Adder can add two whole runs together pair by pair.
state-graph/level.stones.mission.goal: Each move merges two neighbouring piles, costing their combined weight. Work out the least it costs to merge a row of piles into one.
state-graph/level.stones.mission.how: The sweep arm sends the left part and right part for every split point. The robot scans by length, shortest first, so once the circuit is built you can run it.
state-graph/level.stones.tasks.stones.hi: Look at a single split point first: before the last merge, where are the costs of merging the left part and the right part each into one pile? How should they be combined?
Pick the cheapest of all the split points (min), then add this run’s total weight.
state-graph/level.stones.title: Merging stones
state-graph/level.tagging.debrief.body.0: For every part of speech in every column, the table holds “the cheapest explanation up to here”. The smallest cell in the last column is the best tagging of the whole sentence; trace back along the green cells and you can read off each word’s part of speech.
state-graph/level.tagging.debrief.body.1: This is the Viterbi algorithm. Speech recognition turning sound into words, and phone keyboards turning pinyin into Chinese words, both use this table: one column per moment, one row per possibility.
state-graph/level.tagging.debrief.note: Viterbi: each row of the previous column + the cost of following it, take the min, then add the cost of tagging this word this way.
state-graph/level.tagging.debrief.title: The Viterbi algorithm
state-graph/level.tagging.intro.0.t: A new chapter, putting dynamic programming to work on sentences. In “he studies history”, “studies” is a verb; in “these studies”, it is a noun. How does a computer decide the part of speech of every word in a sentence?
state-graph/level.tagging.intro.1.t: Two clues: the cost of a word taking a given part of speech (“studies” is more often a verb, so that costs less), and the cost of one part of speech following another (a verb after a noun is natural, cost 0; another noun after a noun costs 3). The cost of the whole sentence is all of these added up. Pick the tagging with the smallest total cost.
state-graph/level.tagging.intro.2.t: It is a table again: rows are the three parts of speech, columns are the words of the sentence, and on the far left is “start”, holding 0. Cell (part of speech, word k) records: with the words before it tagged, and this word tagged as this part of speech, the least it can cost. The small number in a cell’s corner is the cost of this word taking this part of speech; × means it can’t.
state-graph/level.tagging.intro.3.t: Look only at the last step: the previous word could be any of the three parts of speech. For each possibility, which cell of the table and which fact in the This cell panel do you need? Of the three, which one do you want? The robot reads the previous word’s three cells with its telescopic arm; before the first word there is only “start”, so the arm reads just that cell, and the “after a noun” fact is then the cost of starting the sentence.
state-graph/level.tagging.mission.goal: Work out the smallest total cost of tagging the whole sentence: the cost of each word taking its part of speech, plus the cost of each pair of neighbouring parts of speech.
state-graph/level.tagging.mission.how: The This cell panel has the costs “after a noun / verb / adjective” and “this word, this tag”. Once you pass, see the tagging traced back from the table.
state-graph/level.tagging.short: Is each word a noun or a verb?
If the previous word is a noun, the least cost up to it is in the “previous word as a noun” cell. Going on from there to this word, which cost do you add?
Take the min of the three, then add the “this word, this tag” cost.
“imports” was tagged as a verb: on its own, noun and verb cost the same; it was the words after it that made the verb win.
state-graph/level.tagging.title: Guess the part of speech
state-graph/level.threekeys.debrief.body: Three keys, 8 layers; ten keys, 1,024; twenty, over a million. Every extra thing remembered doubles the table.
state-graph/level.threekeys.intro.0.t: Three keys and doors of three colours. The state remembers all three keys: how many layers in all?
state-graph/level.threekeys.mission.goal: Work out the number of valid routes: the end cells of every layer, added up.
state-graph/level.threekeys.mission.how: Every cell works out every layer.
state-graph/level.threekeys.short: Every extra thing doubles the table
state-graph/level.threekeys.title: Three keys
state-graph/level.trace.debrief.body.0: With only 4 places on the map, tracing routes one by one isn’t too tiring.
state-graph/level.trace.debrief.body.1: But add a few more places and there are too many routes to trace, and it is easy to miss one or count one twice.
state-graph/level.trace.debrief.note: A route = a sequence of places leading from the start to the end along the arrows.
state-graph/level.trace.debrief.title: 3 routes in all
state-graph/level.trace.intro.0.t: Here is a map of a small town. Each place is a cell and each one-way street is an arrow, and you can only travel the way the arrows point.
state-graph/level.trace.intro.1.t: A route is a sequence of places that starts at Home, follows the arrows stop by stop, and ends at School. For example: Home → Bakery → School.
state-graph/level.trace.intro.2.t: Find every route yourself: start at “Home”, click places one after another along the arrows, and each time you reach “School” a route is recorded.
state-graph/level.trace.mission.goal: Find all the routes from Home to School. You can only go the way the arrows point (one-way streets).
state-graph/level.trace.mission.how: Start at “Home” and click places in order along the arrows. If you click a wrong one, click the last place again to step back.
state-graph/level.trace.short: Trace them one by one on a one-way map
state-graph/level.trace.title: Find the routes
With two directions, every cell looks only right and down.
state-graph/level.treasure.debrief.title: The grid world, simplified
state-graph/level.treasure.intro.0.t: A new map: the robot can only go right or down. The treasure is worth 10, and the edge of the map is a ring of cliffs at −10.
state-graph/level.treasure.intro.1.t: Each cell’s value = the better of the cells to the right and below, discounted to 90%.
state-graph/level.treasure.mission.goal: Work out the value of every cell: the better of right and down × 0.9.
state-graph/level.treasure.mission.how: The robot scans in rounds until the table stops changing. The answer is the start cell.
state-graph/level.treasure.tasks.treasur: On this map you only move right or down: up and left can’t be reached.
Right or down only: wire right and down into a max, then multiply by 0.9.
state-graph/level.treasure.title: Treasure, right or down
state-graph/level.twokeys.debrief.body.0: Two keys, four possibilities: none, only red, only blue, both. One layer for each, so the table has 4 layers, yet the circuit board didn’t change at all.
state-graph/level.twokeys.debrief.title: The state shapes the table
state-graph/level.twokeys.intro.0.t: This level has a red key and a blue key, and red and blue doors. Before going through a door, you must have picked up the key of its colour.
state-graph/level.twokeys.intro.1.t: A route can be holding its keys in four ways: none, only red, only blue, or both. So the table is stacked 4 layers deep, each holding the routes “carrying exactly these keys”.
state-graph/level.twokeys.mission.goal: Only right or down. Work out the number of valid routes: the end cells of the four layers, added up.
state-graph/level.twokeys.mission.how: Every cell works out all four layers.
Try the board from <level-ref to="state-graph/keydoor"></level-ref> first.
state-graph/level.twokeys.title: Two keys
state-graph/level.twoorders.debrief.body: By length, row by row from the bottom up, column by column from the bottom up: they all work. They have just one thing in common: every cell comes after the cells it reads.
The order is not part of the answer, just an arrangement of “who goes first”.
state-graph/level.twoorders.debrief.note: Any order works, as long as the cells being read are computed first.
state-graph/level.twoorders.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="state-graph/stones"></level-ref> the robot scanned by length. Would another order work too?
state-graph/level.twoorders.intro.1.t: This level has two tasks on the same circuit board: in task 1 the robot scans by length; in task 2 it switches to row by row, from the bottom up. Both orders have to come out right.
state-graph/level.twoorders.intro.2.t: The <part-ref to="state-graph/interval"></part-ref> is already in your Parts, ready to go on the board. Each cell reads the whole row to its left and the whole column below it: do both orders get those computed first?
state-graph/level.twoorders.mission.goal: Merge the stones as cheaply as possible. Pass once under each of two scan orders, with the same circuit board.
state-graph/level.twoorders.mission.how: In task 1 the robot scans by length; in task 2 the board stays and the robot switches to row by row from the bottom up.
state-graph/level.twoorders.tasks.twoord: Same board; the robot now scans row by row from the bottom up. Pass again.
Put down an <part-ref to="state-graph/interval"></part-ref>, and wire the sweep arm’s left parts and right parts and This cell’s run weight to its three ports.
Each cell reads the cells to its left on the same row and the cells below it in the same column: scanning by length, or row by row from the bottom up, those cells have always been computed first.
Build the circuit board and pass the tests, scanning by length.
The board stays. The robot switches to row by row from the bottom up; run it again.
Put down an <part-ref to="state-graph/interval"></part-ref>, and wire the sweep arm’s left parts and right parts and This cell’s run weight to its three ports.
Each cell reads the cells to its left on the same row and the cells below it in the same column: scanning by length, or row by row from the bottom up, those cells have always been computed first.
state-graph/level.twoorders.title: More than one order
state-graph/level.value.debrief.body.0: Each cell’s number says how good it is to head for the treasure from there: every step further away knocks off another 10%. Traps are −10, and nobody walks into one, so they can’t drag their neighbours down either.
state-graph/level.value.debrief.body.1: This is one of the first cornerstones of reinforcement learning, called . Programs that play board games and robots learning to walk all have to learn to estimate “how good is it to stand here” first. The method is the same old one: look at the neighbours, take the best, write it down.
state-graph/level.value.debrief.note: Value iteration: each cell = the best neighbour × a discount, scanned until nothing changes.
state-graph/level.value.debrief.title: Value iteration
state-graph/level.value.intro.0.t: A map has treasure (value 10), traps (value −10) and walls. The robot wants to know: on each cell, how good is it to stand there?
state-graph/level.value.intro.1.t: The closer to the treasure, the better. The rule: each cell’s value = the largest of its four neighbours, discounted by 10% (× 0.9). Next to the treasure it is 9, one step further 8.1, then 7.29…
state-graph/level.value.intro.2.t: The discount takes a <part-ref to="part:table/mul"></part-ref> (you met it in <level-ref to="state-graph/safefrog"></level-ref>). In this level a Constant can be set to 0.9.
state-graph/level.value.intro.3.t: Every cell starts at 0. The robot scans round after round until the whole table stops changing.
state-graph/level.value.mission.goal: Each cell’s value = the largest value among its four neighbours × 0.9. Treasure is 10, traps are −10, and walls can’t be entered. Work out the value of every cell.
state-graph/level.value.mission.how: This level checks the whole table. Once a Constant is on the board, click it to change it to 0.9.
state-graph/level.value.short: How good is it to stand here
state-graph/level.value.tasks.value.diag: Each step further away is discounted by 10%: use a Multiplier to multiply the best neighbour by 0.9.
state-graph/level.value.tasks.value.hint: Wire all four neighbours into “max”: a Merger has only three inputs, so chain two of them.
Then multiply the largest by 0.9: wire the max into one side of a Multiplier and a Constant 0.9 into the other.
state-graph/level.value.title: The grid world
state-graph/level.wordbreak.debrief.body: A search engine that meets bestbuy, or a Chinese input method given a run of pinyin with no spaces, has to break it into words first.
Try every cut and keep the cheapest: the number of ways in changes with the data, and the table fills all the same.
state-graph/level.wordbreak.intro.0.t: A string of letters with no spaces, such as catsanddog. Cut it into dictionary words: how few parts will do?
state-graph/level.wordbreak.intro.1.t: Cell i records: the fewest parts the first i letters can be cut into. Cell 0 is the start, with no letters at all: 0 parts.
state-graph/level.wordbreak.intro.2.t: Look only at the last part: it starts at some earlier cut and ends here. The sweep arm sweeps every earlier cut and brings two runs at once: the cell at each cut, and what the part from there to here costs. In this level a part that is a word costs 1, and one that isn’t is “—”.
state-graph/level.wordbreak.mission.goal: Work out the fewest dictionary words each string can be cut into.
state-graph/level.wordbreak.mission.how: The dictionary is shown next to the tests.
state-graph/level.wordbreak.short: Every part must be a word
state-graph/level.wordbreak.tasks.wordbr: The arm’s second run is each part’s cost: a part that isn’t a word is “—”, and the Adder drops it.
At every cut: the fewest parts up to there + this part. An Adder adds two runs up item by item.
Take the smallest over all the cuts. The start is 0 parts: let a 0 through with “is start”.
state-graph/level.wordbreak.title: The fewest parts
In <level-ref to="state-graph/wordbreak"></level-ref> every part cost 1, so it counted parts. Change the costs, and the same board finds the cheapest cut.
state-graph/level.wordcost.debrief.title: New costs, the same circuit
state-graph/level.wordcost.intro.0.t: Common words are cheap and rare ones dear: every word in the dictionary has a cost. A way of cutting costs the sum of its parts; find the cheapest.
state-graph/level.wordcost.intro.1.t: The way with the fewest parts is not always the cheapest.
state-graph/level.wordcost.mission.goal: Work out what the cheapest way to cut each string costs.
state-graph/level.wordcost.mission.how: The dictionary and its costs are shown next to the tests.
state-graph/level.wordcost.short: Every part has its own cost
state-graph/level.wordcost.tasks.wordcos: Compared with <level-ref to="state-graph/wordbreak"></level-ref>, only each part’s cost has changed.
state-graph/level.wordcost.title: Some words cost more
state-graph/part.align.desc: One word along the top, the other down the left. If the letters match, up-left + 1; otherwise the larger of up and left.
state-graph/part.align.name: Alignment Table
state-graph/part.anyorder.desc: Any order works, as long as every cell comes after the cells it reads.
state-graph/part.anyorder.name: Many Orders
state-graph/part.choose.desc: Outputs the larger of “keep” and “swap for” plus “plus”.
state-graph/part.choose.name: Best Choice
state-graph/part.cost.desc: Outputs the smallest of: the smallest of up, left and up-left, plus 1; up-left itself when the letters match; 0 on the start.
state-graph/part.cost.name: Edit Distance Meter
state-graph/part.counter.desc: Adds up the numbers on its two ways in, plus 1 when its “start” port is “yes”. A “—” is left out; with nothing to add, it outputs “—”.
state-graph/part.counter.name: Route Counter
state-graph/part.expect.desc: When the outcome is uncertain, weight each outcome by how likely it is, then compare.
state-graph/part.expect.name: Expectation
state-graph/part.interval.desc: Its left and right parts are two runs of numbers: it adds them split point by split point, takes the smallest, then adds the cost of the whole run.
state-graph/part.interval.name: Interval Merger
state-graph/part.judge.desc: Reads the three positions the opponent could face: if any of them is a loss, this cell is a win; otherwise a loss.
state-graph/part.judge.name: Win/Lose Judge
state-graph/part.layer.desc: Copy the table into several layers, so the state remembers one more thing that affects the future.
state-graph/part.layer.name: Layers
state-graph/part.local.desc: Anything below 0 is cut to 0: starting afresh beats carrying a negative score along. The answer is the largest cell in the table.
state-graph/part.local.name: Local Alignment
state-graph/part.min.desc: Takes the smallest of up to three ways in (when its “start” port is “yes”, 0 counts as a way in too), then adds this cell’s cost. When every way in is “—”, it outputs “—”.
state-graph/part.min.name: Cheapest Cell
state-graph/part.order.desc: Every cell must come after the cells it reads. Reverse the order, and the directions the circuit reads must reverse too.
state-graph/part.order.name: Fill Order
state-graph/part.roll.desc: Keep just one row and rewrite it in place. The direction you rewrite in decides how many times each item can be used.
state-graph/part.roll.name: Rolling Array
state-graph/part.seam.desc: Each cell = its own energy + the smallest of the three cells above it. Trace back from the smallest cell in the bottom row, and cut that seam out.
state-graph/part.seam.name: Seam Carving
state-graph/part.sweep.desc: Reads a whole run of cells at once. But sweeping from the start on every cell is slow: if the previous cell has already stored the answer, use it instead of sweeping again.
state-graph/part.sweep.name: Sweep Arm
state-graph/part.value.desc: Takes the largest of up to four ways in, then multiplies it by the number set on its part (0.9, say).
state-graph/part.value.name: Discounter
state-graph/part.viterbi.desc: For every tag in every column, keep the cheapest explanation up to here: each row of the previous column plus its transition cost, then the min.
state-graph/part.viterbi.name: Viterbi
state-graph/part.wordbreak.desc: If some earlier position can be split and the part from there to here is exactly a word, this position can be split too.
state-graph/part.wordbreak.name: Word Breaker

table/capability.robot.items.robot-broom: Vision 3×3, plus a sweep arm: it sweeps a whole run of cells in one go and feeds every number in the run into the circuit board, however many cells the run has.

table/capability.robot.items.robot-scout: Vision 3×3: it sees the ring of 8 cells around it.
table/capability.robot.items.robot-stack: It stands on many layers at once: however many layers the table has, it works once on the same cell of each. Every layer has a 3×3 view, and its probe reaches cells on another layer.

table/glossary.entries.arms.body.0: Longarm has a telescopic arm: how far it reaches depends on the cell’s own data, such as reaching left by as many cells as “this item’s weight”, so it can read cells outside its view.
table/glossary.entries.arms.body.1: Under the view is the arm’s own row, showing the cells it can reach; click one, and the “View” part gains an output that reads it.
table/glossary.entries.arms.title: Telescopic arm
table/glossary.entries.cells.body.0: To begin with you have just two things: cells and arrows. A cell holds a number; an arrow carries the number in the cell it starts from into the cell it ends at.
table/glossary.entries.cells.body.1: When several arrows point at the same cell, the cell adds up everything it receives; a cell no arrow points at holds 0.
table/glossary.entries.cells.body.2: To draw an arrow, click one cell and then another; connect the same two cells again and the arrow is removed. A cell can only be worked out once every arrow pointing at it has delivered, so arrows must never loop round.
table/glossary.entries.cells.title: Cells and arrows
table/glossary.entries.dial.body.0: The robot walks the table in a scan order: row by row from the top left, row by row from the bottom right… Each level’s introduction tells you how it walks.
table/glossary.entries.dial.body.1: The order has to follow the circuit: a cell that is read must come before the cell that reads it. A circuit that reads right and down has to start from the bottom right.
table/glossary.entries.dial.title: Scan order
table/glossary.entries.dirs.body.0: In levels that keep a single row and rewrite it in place, the machine rewrites that row in one rewrite direction: right to left when each item can be taken at most once, left to right when each can be taken many times.
table/glossary.entries.dirs.body.1: During a run, yellow marks the cell being rewritten, and red means a cell read a value that was rewritten earlier in the same pass. The direction decides whether a cell reads an old value or a new one, and so what the row means.
table/glossary.entries.dirs.title: Rewrite direction
table/glossary.entries.sweep.body.0: Broom has a sweep arm: it sweeps a whole run of cells in one go and feeds every number in the run into the circuit board, however many cells the run has.
table/glossary.entries.sweep.body.1: A wire carrying a whole segment is drawn thicker. Mergers, Adders and Multipliers take a whole segment directly, and every number in it takes part; gates do not take segments.
table/glossary.entries.sweep.title: Sweep Arm
table/glossary.entries.testBoard.body.0: Before a run, the test board is a place to try things out: click a cell to type a number into it, or to send the robot there, and the red frame shows the circuit board’s answer for that cell straight away. On a computer you can type the digits, press Enter to confirm and Esc to put the keypad away.
table/glossary.entries.testBoard.body.1: Click Run tests and the board is cleared; the robot starts again and walks it in the scan order, one test after another. If a test fails, the robot stops on the cell that went wrong: the numbers in the view and on the circuit board are what it saw and worked out there.
table/glossary.entries.testBoard.body.2: After a run, click any computed cell to see what the machine worked out there, and click again to leave it; “Back to the test board” takes you back to trying things out. Some levels only check the answer cell and some check the whole table; “How to play” says which.
table/glossary.entries.testBoard.title: Test board
